會試錄序

今皇上膺天命，光復寶祚，紀元之春，適當會試之期。天下士領薦書而至者，盖三千餘人。禮部左侍郎臣榦等以考試官請，上命臣瑄、臣原往涖其事。同考官臣溥、臣賢、臣泰、臣正、臣佖、臣恂、臣𧷢、臣節、臣淳、臣鏞，監試御史臣烈、臣鑑，暨百執事，罔不夙夜祗承。凡三試，得文之中程式者若干名，并擇其文
translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Metropolitan Examination

In the spring of the first year of the reign period in which the present Emperor received the Mandate of Heaven and gloriously restored the Imperial Throne, it happened to be the scheduled time for the Metropolitan Examination. The scholars of the realm who arrived bearing letters of recommendation numbered more than three thousand in all. When Your Servant Gan 榦, Left Vice Minister of Rites, and others requested the appointment of Examiners, the Emperor commanded Your Servant Xuan 瑄 and Your Servant Yuan 原 to go and preside over the affair. The Associate Examiners—Your Servant Pu 溥, Your Servant Xian 賢, Your Servant Tai 泰, Your Servant Zheng 正, Your Servant Bi 佖, Your Servant Xun 恂, Your Servant Zhan 𧷢, Your Servant Jie 節, Your Servant Chun 淳, and Your Servant Yong 鏞—the Monitoring Censors Your Servant Lie 烈 and Your Servant Jian 鑑, together with all the officiating functionaries, none failed to attend reverently to their duties day and night. Across the three examination sessions in all, we obtained a certain number of candidates whose essays met the prescribed standards, and we also selected from their essays…

title: 天順元年會試錄
text:
之尤粹者彙而成錄臣切惟
為治莫先於得賢養士必本
於正學而正學者復其固有
之性是已性復則明體適用
大而負經濟之任細而釐百
司之務焉往而不得其當哉
故三代小大之學養士之法
===
皆以復性為本其得賢致治
之效盖可考矣漢唐以来正
學緒微養士不本於復性往
往溺於雜學術數記誦詞章
之習體有不明用有不周雖
或有傑出之才亦不過隨所
學以就功名而已其視三代

===

之效蓋可考矣漢唐以来正
學緒徼養士不本於復性往
往溺於雜學術數記誦詞章

或有傑出之才亦不過隨所
學以就功名而巳其視三代
punctuated: 之尤粹者，彙而成錄。臣切惟：為治莫先於得賢，養士必本於正學。而正學者，復其固有之性是已。性復則明體適用，大而負經濟之任，細而釐百司之務，焉往而不得其當哉！故三代小大之學、養士之法，皆以復性為本，其得賢致治之效，盖可考矣。漢唐以来，正學緒微，養士不本於復性，往往溺於雜學、術數、記誦、詞章之習，體有不明，用有不周。雖或有傑出之才，亦不過隨所學以就功名而已，其視三代
translation_en:
… the purest among them, compiling them into a record.

Your servant humbly reflects: In governance, nothing takes precedence over obtaining worthy men, and nurturing scholars must be rooted in orthodox learning. Orthodox learning is simply recovering one's inherent nature. When one's nature is recovered, one comprehends the fundamental substance and is suited for practical application; in great matters, one can shoulder the responsibility of ordering the state and benefiting the people, and in small matters, one can regulate the affairs of the hundred offices—where could one go and not handle things appropriately? Therefore, in the lesser and greater learning of the Three Dynasties, the methods of nurturing scholars all took the recovery of nature as their foundation, and the efficacy of their obtaining worthy men and achieving good governance can indeed be verified. From the Han and Tang dynasties onward, the thread of orthodox learning grew faint. The nurturing of scholars was not rooted in recovering nature, and men frequently drowned in the habits of eclectic learning, prognostic techniques, rote memorization, andbelletristic composition. Their grasp of substance was not clear, and their practical application was not comprehensive. Even when there were occasionally outstanding talents, they did no more than follow what they had learned to achieve personal merit and fame; compared to the Three Dynasties'…

title: 天順元年會試錄
text:
之賢才為何如哉至宋道學
諸君子出其論養士之法始
皆本於復性雖其說不得盡
行於當時而實有待於
盛世洪惟
天眷
皇明
===
列聖相繼大建學校慎選師儒其
養士之法必以三代孔孟程
朱復性之說為本是以九十
餘年薄海内外文教隆洽士
習粹然一出天理民彝之正
而雜學術數記誦詞章之習
剗刮消磨無復前季之陋雖

punctuated: 之賢才為何如哉？至宋道學諸君子出，其論養士之法，始皆本於復性。雖其說不得盡行於當時，而實有待於盛世。洪惟天眷皇明，列聖相繼，大建學校，慎選師儒。其養士之法，必以三代、孔、孟、程、朱復性之說為本。是以九十餘年，薄海内外，文教隆洽，士習粹然，一出天理民彝之正，而雜學術數、記誦詞章之習，剗刮消磨，無復前季之陋。雖
translation_en: …how do they compare to the worthy talents of the Three Dynasties? When the gentlemen of the Learning of the Way (Daoxue) emerged in the Song dynasty, their discussions on the method of nurturing scholars for the first time all took returning to one's original nature as the foundation. Although their doctrines could not be fully put into practice in their own time, in truth they awaited a flourishing age. Reflecting deeply on how Heaven has favored the August Ming: the successive sagely emperors have followed one after another, establishing schools on a grand scale and carefully selecting teachers and Confucian masters. Their method of nurturing scholars invariably takes the doctrines of returning to one's original nature from the Three Dynasties, Confucius, Mencius, the Cheng brothers (Cheng Hao and Cheng Yi), and Zhu Xi as its foundation. Therefore, for more than ninety years, within and beyond the four seas, cultural education has been prosperous and harmonious, and the ethos of scholars has become pure, issuing entirely from the correctness of Heavenly principle and the constant norms of the people; meanwhile, the habits of eclectic learning, numerology and techniques, rote memorization, and華麗 belles-lettres have been pared away and worn down, leaving nothing of the vulgarity of former ages. Although…

title: 天順元年會試錄
text:
曰科目以文章取士然必根
於義理能發明性之體用者
始與選列類非詞章無本者
之可擬也故其得賢致治之
效足以追隆前古今諸士子
荷
朝廷正學教養之恩既以有本
===
之文得在選列行見對于
大廷益當以明體適用自勵隨所
器使以忠乎
國以愛乎民以贊助
皇明重煕累洽之治於無窮俾正
學得賢之效有光於前有垂
於後顧不偉歟

punctuated: 曰科目以文章取士，然必根於義理，能發明性之體用者，始與選列，類非詞章無本者之可擬也。故其得賢致治之效，足以追隆前古。今諸士子荷朝廷正學教養之恩，既以有本之文得在選列，行見對于大廷，益當以明體適用自勵，隨所器使，以忠乎國，以愛乎民，以贊助皇明重煕累洽之治於無窮，俾正學得賢之效，有光於前，有垂於後，顧不偉歟！
translation_en: … the recruitment system selects scholars through literary compositions, only those whose writings are rooted in moral principle and can elucidate the substance and function of human nature are included on the list of the chosen—altogether incomparable to rootless belles-lettres. Therefore, its effectiveness in obtaining worthy men and bringing about good governance is sufficient to rival the flourishing eras of antiquity. Now that these examination candidates, having received the Court's grace of education and nurturing in orthodox learning, have been placed among the chosen by virtue of their well-grounded writings, they are soon to respond to the Emperor in the Great Court. All the more should they spur themselves on to clarify fundamental substance and apply it to practical governance. In whatever capacity they are employed, they should be loyal to the dynasty, cherish the people, and assist in perpetuating the August Ming's governance of cumulative splendor and pervasive harmony without end, so that the efficacy of orthodox learning in obtaining worthy men will shine upon the past and be handed down to posterity. Would that not be magnificent indeed?

punctuated:
禮、樂，皆所謂經世之典，以立人極者也。洪惟我太祖高皇帝統一寰區，稽古為治，乃於萬幾之暇，御製《大誥》三編，有申明五常、五教育民之訓，其與古經世之典以立人極者同歟？太宗文皇帝御製《為善陰隲》、《孝順事實》，宣宗章皇帝御製《五倫書》，其曰善、曰孝、曰五倫，又與《大誥》五常、五教立人極之旨同歟？諸士子明陳其說，以觀博古通今之學。

問：天下之理一也。若《易》、《書》、《詩》、《春秋》、《禮》、《樂》，其為教雖不同，而其理果同歟？《大學》、《論》、《孟》、《中庸》，其為書雖不同，而其理又同歟？《太極圖說》、《通書》、《西銘》，三書之理又果同歟？朱子謂孟子「性善」之說，旁通七篇之義，無非此理。誠欲會六經、四書、《太極圖說》、《通書》、《西銘》為一理，亦有一言可以盡兼其義歟？諸士子試陳其說。
translation_en:
… the Record of Rites, and the Classic of Music—all are what have been called statecraft canons that establish the ultimate standard for humanity.

Reflecting deeply upon our Grand Progenitor, Emperor Gao (Taizu, the Hongwu Emperor), who unified the realm and examined antiquity in order to govern: in his leisure from a myriad of state affairs, he imperially composed the three parts of the Grand Pronouncements (Dagao), which contain instructions clarifying the Five Constant Virtues and Five Teachings to nurture the people. Are these identical with the ancient statecraft canons that established the ultimate standard for humanity? The Grand Ancestor, Emperor Wen (Taizong, the Yongle Emperor), imperially composed the Hidden Rewards of Doing Good (Weishan yinzhi) and the True Records of Filial Piety (Xiaoshun shishi), and the Proclaiming Ancestor, Emperor Zhang (Xuanzong, the Xuande Emperor), imperially composed the Book of the Five Human Relationships (Wulun shu). In speaking of goodness, filial piety, and the five human relationships, are their aims again identical with the Five Constant Virtues and Five Teachings of the Grand Pronouncements in establishing the ultimate standard for humanity? Let the candidates clearly set forth their explanations, so that we may observe their learning that encompasses both antiquity and the present.

Question: The principle of all under heaven is one. As for the Book of Changes, the Book of Documents, the Book of Odes, the Spring and Autumn Annals, the Record of Rites, and the Classic of Music—although the teachings they offer differ, is their underlying principle indeed the same? As for the Great Learning, the Analects, the Mencius, and the Doctrine of the Mean—although they differ as books, is their principle also the same? And is the principle of the three works—the Explanation of the Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate (Taijitu shuo), the Penetrating the Book of Changes (Tongshu), and the Western Inscription (Ximing)—indeed the same as well? Master Zhu (Zhu Xi) said that Mencius's doctrine of the goodness of human nature permeates the meaning of all seven chapters of his book, and that none of it is anything other than this principle. If one truly wished to bring together the Six Classics, the Four Books, the Explanation of the Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate, the Penetrating the Book of Changes, and the Western Inscription into a single principle, is there also a single phrase that can fully encompass their meaning? Let the candidates try to set forth their explanations.

之法若堯舜禹湯文武之精一執中建
中建極者為治之道也分五服爵五等
建百官脩五禮審律呂定田賦設學校
慎選舉立兵制明刑罰者為治之法也
然在當時其為治之道與法今亦可詳
考其根本節目歟夫為治之道萬古而
不易為治之法因時以制宜自漢唐宋
以來凡封建官制禮樂田賦學校選舉

學
===
問格物致知儒者第一事也姑舉所疑者
言之邵子有言天開於子地闢於丑且
天地未闢之前既無曆書以紀數又何
以知其爲子丑乎周子曰太極動而生
陽其未動之前又果有何物乎月之上
明先儒謂受日之光其果然乎揚子
punctuated:
問：古帝王之治天下，有為治之道，有為治之法。若堯、舜、禹、湯、文、武之「精一執中」、「建中」、「建極」者，為治之道也；分五服、爵五等、建百官、脩五禮、審律呂、定田賦、設學校、慎選舉、立兵制、明刑罰者，為治之法也。然在當時，其為治之道與法，今亦可詳考其根本節目歟？夫為治之道，萬古而不易；為治之法，因時以制宜。自漢、唐、宋以來，凡封建、官制、禮樂、田賦、學校、選舉、兵刑之法，因時而制宜者，亦有遠合先王之遺意者歟？試詳陳之，以觀用世之學。

問：格物致知，儒者第一事也。姑舉所疑者言之：邵子有言：「天開於子，地闢於丑。」且天地未闢之前，既無曆書以紀數，又何以知其為子、丑乎？周子曰：「太極動而生陽。」其未動之前，又果有何物乎？月之生明，先儒謂受日之光，其果然乎？揚子□
translation_en:
Question: When the emperors and kings of antiquity governed All under Heaven, they possessed the Way of governance and they possessed the methods of governance. Such principles as Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, King Wen, and King Wu's "being refined and single-minded, holding fast to the mean" (jingyi zhizhong), "establishing the mean" (jianzhong), and "establishing the supreme standard" (jianji) were the Way of governance; demarcating the Five Zones (wufu), conferring the five ranks of nobility, establishing the hundred officials, cultivating the five rites, examining the pitch-pipes (lülü), fixing land taxes, setting up schools, exercising care in selection and recommendation (xuanju), instituting military systems, and clarifying punishments and penalties were the methods of governance. Yet as for their Way and methods of governance in those times, can we today still examine their fundamental principles and detailed provisions in full? Now, the Way of governance does not change through ten thousand ages, whereas the methods of governance are adapted to the times as appropriate. Since the Han, Tang, and Song dynasties, among all the methods concerning enfeoffment (fengjian), official systems, rites and music, land taxes, schools, selection and recommendation, and military and penal affairs that were adapted to the times as appropriate, were there also those that across the ages accorded with the surviving intentions of the former kings? Try to set them forth in detail, so that we may observe your learning for practical service to the world.

Question: Investigating things and extending knowledge (gewu zhizhi) is the foremost business of the Confucian scholar. Let us tentatively raise some points of doubt to discuss: Master Shao [Shao Yong 邵雍] said, "Heaven opened in the zi period, and Earth was cleared in the chou period." Yet before Heaven and Earth were opened and cleared, since there were no calendrical treatises to record the numbers, how could one know that they were zi and chou? Master Zhou [Zhou Dunyi 周敦頤] said, "The Supreme Ultimate (Taiji) moves and generates yang." Before it moved, what thing was really there? As for the moon's generating brightness, former Confucians held that it receives the light of the sun; is this truly so? Master Yang [Yang Xiong 楊雄] [?]…

text:
未望載於西旣望終於東又曰遡日以
為明其曰載曰終曰遡果何義乎先天
圖乃伏羲所作易中一字一義皆出於
此程子作易傳何無一語以及之乎且
伏羲畫卦大禹叙疇皆取法於河圖洛
書者也周子非有所取法又何從而作
太極圖乎說者謂太極圖源出於希夷
果信然乎張忠定言公事有陰陽其即
太極圖之意乎夫人得天地之理以成
===

質之論乎且氣質之性於太極圖其有
合乎此皆窮理致知之事試詳辯之

雖為孔門之高第然未有行事之可見
朱子謂其有王佐才故問為邦使其達
而在上果能為伊傅周召之事業歟先

問古伊傅周召之徒皆三王之佐也顏子
雖為孔門之高第然未有行事之可見
朱子謂其有王佐才故問為邦使其達
而在上果能為伊傅周召之事業歟先
儒謂諸葛孔明有王佐才又何以見之
歟夫士君子之竭力盡忠者非先正之
punctuated:
未望載於西，旣望終於東，又曰「遡日以為明」，其曰載、曰終、曰遡，果何義乎？《先天圖》乃伏羲所作，《易》中一字一義皆出於此，程子作《易傳》，何無一語以及之乎？且伏羲畫卦、大禹叙疇，皆取法於《河圖》、《洛書》者也，周子非有所取法，又何從而作《太極圖》乎？說者謂《太極圖》源出於希夷，果信然乎？張忠定言「公事有陰陽」，其即《太極圖》之意乎？夫人得天地之理以成性，有善而無惡者也，先儒又何以有氣質之論乎？且氣質之性於《太極圖》，其有合乎？此皆窮理致知之事，試詳辯之。
問：古伊、傅、周、召之徒，皆三王之佐也。顏子雖為孔門之高第，然未有行事之可見，朱子謂其有王佐才，故問為邦。使其達而在上，果能為伊、傅、周、召之事業歟？先儒謂諸葛孔明有王佐才，又何以見之歟？夫士君子之竭力盡忠者，非先正之
translation_en:
… "before the full moon it begins to shine in the west, and after the full moon it ends in the east," and also says that "it faces the sun to gain its brightness." What indeed is the meaning of these terms "begins to shine" (zai), "ends" (zhong), and "faces" (su)? The Diagram of Preceding Heaven (Xiantian tu) was created by Fuxi 伏羲, and every word and meaning in the Classic of Changes (Yi) derives from it. When Master Cheng 程子 composed his Commentary on the Changes (Yi zhuan), why did he not mention a single word about it? Furthermore, when Fuxi drew the trigrams and Great Yu 大禹 arranged the Nine Categories, both took as their models the Yellow River Chart (Hetu) and the Luo River Writing (Luoshu). Since Master Zhou 周子 (Zhou Dunyi 周敦頤) had no such models to follow, from where did he derive the Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate (Taiji tu)? Commentators say that the Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate originated with Xiyi 希夷 (Chen Tuan 陳摶); is this truly so? Zhang Zhongding 張忠定 (Zhang Yong 張詠) said that "official business has yin and yang"; is this the very meaning of the Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate? Now, human beings receive the principle of Heaven and Earth to form their nature, which is wholly good and without evil. Why then did former Confucians propose the theory of psychophysical endowment (qizhi)? Moreover, does the nature of psychophysical endowment accord with the Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate? All of these are matters of fathoming principle and extending knowledge; try to analyze them in detail.

Question: In antiquity, men such as Yi Yin 伊尹, Fu Yue 傅說, the Duke of Zhou 周公, and the Duke of Shao 召公 were all assistants to the Three Kings. Although Master Yan 顏子 (Yan Hui 顏回) was the foremost disciple of the Confucian school, he left no visible record of practical achievements. Master Zhu 朱子 (Zhu Xi 朱熹) said that he possessed the talent to assist a true king, which is why he asked about governing a state. Had he attained high office, could he indeed have accomplished the deeds of Yi Yin, Fu Yue, the Duke of Zhou, and the Duke of Shao? Former Confucians also said that Zhuge Kongming 諸葛孔明 (Zhuge Liang 諸葛亮) possessed the talent to assist a true king; how can this be seen? Now, for scholar-gentlemen who exert their utmost strength and exhaust their loyalty, without the [Way] of the former worthies…

何理為何事而可以庶幾歟

punctuated: 道無以學。誠欲學其道，又當讀何書、明何理、為何事，而可以庶幾歟？
translation_en: … Way, they have nothing from which to learn. If one truly wishes to learn their Way, what books should one read, what principles should one illuminate, and what deeds should one perform so that one might come close to achieving it?

title: 天順元年會試錄
text:
四書
一日克己復禮天下歸仁焉為仁由己而由人
乎哉顏淵曰請問其目子曰非禮勿視非禮勿
聽非禮勿言非禮勿動
吳繹思
同考試官署郎中翁批題本平易難於措辭
此作發越殆無餘蘊可羨可羨
同考試官侍講孫批說理詳明措詞鬯達宜錄
出以為後學之式
===
同考試官少卿錢批仁至難言也而此作化腐
為竒不戾本旨豈有所得而然乎
考試官侍講呂批詞理簡明足見本領之學
考試官學士薛批理明詞整可取
聖人論為仁之效而言機之不預於人答問仁之目
而言欲之當制於己夫為仁必有其效而機則在於
己也苟不惟欲之是制焉又何以見仁果不由乎人
哉宜聖人舉之為大賢告也思昔聖人因顏子問仁
而告之意謂己者一身之私欲也而吾克之如勝敵

四書

「一日克己復禮，天下歸仁焉。為仁由己，而由人乎哉？」顏淵曰：「請問其目。」子曰：「非禮勿視，非禮勿聽，非禮勿言，非禮勿動。」

吳繹思

同考試官、署郎中翁批：題本平易，難於措辭。此作發越，殆無餘蘊。可羨，可羨！
同考試官、侍講孫批：說理詳明，措詞鬯達，宜錄出以為後學之式。
同考試官、少卿錢批：仁至難言也，而此作化腐為竒，不戾本旨，豈有所得而然乎？
考試官、侍講呂批：詞理簡明，足見本領之學。
考試官、學士薛批：理明詞整，可取。

聖人論為仁之效，而言機之不預於人；答問仁之目，而言欲之當制於己。夫為仁必有其效，而機則在於己也。苟不惟欲之是制焉，又何以見仁果不由乎人哉？宜聖人舉之為大賢告也。思昔聖人因顏子問仁而告之，意謂：己者，一身之私欲也，而吾克之如勝敵

"If for one day a man can subdue himself and return to propriety, all under heaven will ascribe benevolence to him. Does the practice of benevolence depend on oneself, or does it depend on others?" Yan Yuan 顏淵 said, "May I ask for the specific items of this?" The Master said, "Look not at what is contrary to propriety; listen not to what is contrary to propriety; speak not what is contrary to propriety; make no movement that is contrary to propriety."

Wu Yisi 吳繹思

Associate Examiner and Acting Director (langzhong) Weng 翁 comments: The topic is inherently plain and simple, making it difficult to phrase an essay on it. This composition develops the theme with vigor, leaving almost no subtle meaning unexpressed. Admirable, admirable!
Associate Examiner and Expositor-in-Waiting (shijiang) Sun 孫 comments: Its explanation of principle is detailed and clear, and its phrasing is fluent and expressive. It ought to be copied out as a model for later students.
Associate Examiner and Vice Minister (shaoqing) Qian 錢 comments: Benevolence is most difficult to speak of, yet this composition turns the commonplace into the extraordinary without violating the original purport. Could it be so because the writer has genuinely grasped something of it?
Examiner and Expositor-in-Waiting (shijiang) Lü 呂 comments: The wording and reasoning are concise and clear, sufficient to show learning of fundamental substance.
Examiner and Academician (xueshi) Xue 薛 comments: The reasoning is clear and the wording well-ordered; it is worthy of selection.

The Sage, in discussing the effect of practicing benevolence, states that its pivotal mechanism does not involve others; in replying to the question about the specific items of benevolence, he states that desires must be regulated by oneself. Now, practicing benevolence necessarily has its effect, yet the pivotal mechanism lies within oneself. If one does not exclusively regulate one's desires, how else could it be seen that benevolence indeed does not depend on others? It is fitting that the Sage raised this to instruct the great worthy. Reflecting on the past, when the Sage instructed Master Yan in response to his question about benevolence, his meaning was that "the self" refers to the selfish desires of one's person, and one subdues them as if vanquishing an enemy…

… Propriety is the regulation and refinement of Heavenly Principle, and I return to it as if returning home. If today I overcome the self and only return to propriety, then today everyone in the world who loves this admirable virtue will without exception grant my benevolence; if tomorrow I return to propriety and there is no selfish ego left to overcome, then tomorrow everyone in the world who shares this innate moral nature will likewise without exception acknowledge my benevolence. Yet although its swiftness takes place within the span of a single day, the pivotal initiative of overcoming and returning is decided by myself alone—where could others apply their effort? Although its greatness reaches the utmost extent of the whole world's approval, the pivotal initiative of overcoming and returning is fulfilled by myself alone—where could others exert their strength? Is this not discussing the efficacy of practicing benevolence while stating that its pivotal initiative does not depend on others?

Yet no sooner had the Sage's discourse ended than Yanzi's mind immediately grasped it; therefore, he had no further doubts or questions, and directly asked for its specific items. Thereupon the Sage answered him again, meaning to say: The eyes govern sight and the ears preside over hearing, and they cannot be free from the entry of what is contrary to propriety; by prohibiting the entry of what is contrary to propriety, one has the means to keep one's benevolence whole. Speech issues from the mouth and movement sprouts in the mind, and they cannot be free from the emergence of what is contrary to propriety; by prohibiting the emergence of what is contrary to propriety, one is able to preserve one's benevolence. Yet overcoming the selfish impulses of sight and hearing so as to return to propriety certainly decides the pivotal initiative that comes from oneself; conquering the desires of speech and movement so as to return to propriety—what part does that have in strength derived from others? Is this not, in turn, answering about the specific items of benevolence while stating that desires ought to be controlled by oneself?

In general, overcoming the self and returning to propriety is the Way of Heaven (Qian). Without the utmost clarity, one cannot discern the subtle pivot between principle and desire; without the utmost vigor, one has no way to achieve the resolve of overcoming and returning. Thus only Yanzi was able to hear this, come close to having no ego, and be the one within the Sage's gate who truly loved learning! Moreover, not deviating from benevolence for three months—what was the mere swiftness of a single day to him? punctuated: 性之郛廓，而性處於心之内，初非由彼以及此也；恭敬之禮、是非之智，亦人之性也，心者性之將帥，而性統於心之中，初非自外而至内也。然性雖在内，而人不知其所以思；性雖固有，而人不知其所當求。殊不知心存而理自得，氣至而理亦至，故弗思則已，而思之有必明；弗求則已，而求之有必得。此其得失之幾在我，而善惡之品所由分焉。所以或一倍、或五倍之相遠，或推而極於無數之可筭，是何也？亦由不思不求，而不能擴充以盡其才耳。夫才為心之用，而萬理無不具；才為性之能，而衆善無不完。使能思而求之，則智足以周萬物之情，必有以全四者之心於已矣；使能擴而充之，則道足以濟天下之衆，必有以遠無筭之譏於人矣。噫！性之得失係於已，而已之善惡由於心，心也者，所以統性情而盡才能者歟！抑考《易》曰「成性」、《書》曰「恒性」、《詩》曰「懿德」，此三代之言性，未甞辯也。時乎戰國，正學弗明，雖以告子之明，不能毆異端之惑。而孟子是懼，不得已折而闢之，以復吾道於既蝕，撥亂世而反之正。謂孟子之功不在禹下，詎不信夫！
translation_en:
…the outer wall of human nature, and human nature resides within the mind; from the beginning it does not reach here from elsewhere. The propriety of reverence and respect, and the wisdom of approving and disapproving, are likewise man's nature. The mind is the commander of human nature, and human nature is governed within the mind; from the beginning it does not enter into the interior from the outside. Yet although human nature is within, people do not know how to reflect upon it; although human nature is inherently theirs, people do not know what they ought to seek. They fail to realize that when the mind is preserved, principle is naturally attained, and where vital energy arrives, principle also arrives. Therefore, if one does not reflect, that is the end of it, but if one reflects upon it, one will surely understand; if one does not seek, that is the end of it, but if one seeks it, one will surely attain it. Thus the pivot of gain and loss lies within oneself, and from this the grades of good and evil are divided. Why is it, then, that men diverge from one another by twice as much, or five times as much, or even to the extreme of incalculable multiples? It is simply because they neither reflect nor seek, and so are unable to expand and fulfill their innate capacities to the utmost.

Now, innate capacity is the function of the mind, in which all principles are fully present; innate capacity is the ability of human nature, in which every goodness is complete. If one is able to reflect and seek it, one's wisdom will suffice to encompass the conditions of the myriad things, and one will surely be able to keep the minds of those four virtues whole within oneself. If one is able to expand and fill it out, one's Way will suffice to bring aid to the multitudes of the world, and one will surely be able to keep far from oneself the reproach among men of falling short by an incalculable measure. Alas! The gain or loss of human nature depends upon oneself, and the goodness or evil of oneself stems from the mind. Is not the mind that which governs nature and the emotions, and brings innate capacities and abilities to their fullest realization?

Moreover, if we examine the Classic of Changes (Yi), which speaks of "completed nature," the Book of Documents (Shu), which speaks of "constant nature," and the Book of Odes (Shi), which speaks of "admirable virtue," we see that in discussing human nature during the Three Dynasties, men never engaged in disputation. By the time of the Warring States, orthodox learning was no longer clear; even with the intelligence of Gaozi, he could not drive away the delusions of heterodox doctrines. Fearing this, Mencius had no choice but to refute and expose them, so as to restore our Way after it had already been eclipsed, bringing order out of a chaotic age and returning it to orthodoxy. When it is said that Mencius's merit was no less than that of Yu, how could that not be true!

text:
其義而贊之哉今夫井之為卦合巽坎而成體六四
一爻以陰居陰雖得其正然陰柔不泉但能脩其舊
井而無及物之功治其敝漏而無濟人之澤故其象
為井甃而其占僅可以免咎也爻易之旨如此而象
傳以為四之所以井甃者不過脩治其井而已然功
未及於物也若九五一爻陽剛中正井道至此初泥
已浚而井極其潔二漏已脩而泉極其寒故足為人
食而功及於物占者必有其德則契其象也爻易之
旨如此象傳以為五之泉所以寒者以其備中正之
===
德而已然功未至於大成也若至上六周公以為井
以上出為功而六居井體之上則為人之汲取卦之
坎口不掩而六處坎口之地則無物之蔽覆是以其
出有源而其用無窮占者必有孚乃元吉也象又申
之蓋謂四之甃而未有功五之食而未成功今既元
吉而居井上則為井功之大成矣爻象聖人各因其
爻而贊其義厥旨深哉抑嘗合井卦而觀之以巽木
入坎水之下故彖曰巽乎水而上水井井養而不窮
也然下三爻皆不為人之食故初井泥二井谷三井

As for the Yin line in the fourth place (Six in the Fourth), although as a Yin line occupying a Yin position it attains correctness, yet being Yin and yielding it does not produce a spring; it can only repair the old well without achieving the merit of reaching creatures, and mend its broken leaks without providing the benefit of aiding people. Therefore, its image is "the well is being lined with stone," and its prognostication is merely that one can avoid blame. Such is the purport of the line statement in the Changes, and the Commentary on the Images (Xiangzhuan) considers that the reason the fourth line is "a well being lined with stone" is simply that it repairs and puts the well in order, though its merit has not yet reached creatures. As for the Yang line in the fifth place (Nine in the Fifth), it is Yang, firm, central, and correct. When the Way of the Well reaches this point, the mud of the first line has already been dredged so that the well is utterly pure, and the leak of the second line has already been repaired so that the spring is utterly cold. Therefore, it is fit to be drunk by people and its merit reaches creatures; the diviner must possess this virtue in order to tally with its image. Such is the purport of the line statement in the Changes, and the Commentary on the Images considers that the reason the spring in the fifth place is cold is simply that it possesses the virtue of centrality and correctness, though its merit has not yet reached great completion. When we come to the Yin line at the top (Six at the Top), the Duke of Zhou considered that a well takes emerging at the top as its merit, and since the Six occupies the top of the body of the well, it is drawn by people; the mouth of the trigram Kan in the hexagram is uncovered, and since the Six occupies the place of the mouth of Kan, nothing covers or obstructs it. Thus its outflow has a source and its use is inexhaustible, and if the diviner has sincerity, there will be supreme good fortune. The Commentary on the Images further elaborates on this, meaning that whereas the fourth line's lining with stone has not yet achieved merit, and the fifth line's being drunk has not yet brought the merit to completion, now that there is "supreme good fortune" and it occupies the top of the well, this represents the great completion of the well's merit. The sages who composed the line statements and the Commentary on the Images each praised the meaning on the basis of the respective line—how profound is their purport! Moreover, if we examine the Jing hexagram as a whole: because Xun (wood) enters beneath Kan (water), the Commentary on the Decision (Tuan) says, "Entering the water and bringing up the water is the Well; the Well nourishes and is not exhausted." title: 天順元年會試錄
text:
有卦焉有爻焉以卦言之必原其事之始要其事之
終事之始終既具卦之體質已成此卦所以有定體
也以爻言之九六迭用剛柔雜居因其時位不同故
其取物亦異此爻所以無定用也聖人言卦爻之體
用如此又以初上二爻而言初為卦之本本則其質
未明故難知上為卦之末末則其質已著故易知惟
其難知也則所繫之辭必擬議而後得惟其易知也
但卒其辭而成其卦之終此初上二爻又為易之一
義也又以中四爻而言如震下坎上其體為屯雜而
===
撰之自二至四互坤也其物為地有順之德焉自三
至五互艮也其物為山有止之德焉五陽位也而以
陽居之則當位而吉固可辯其為是二陰位也而以
陽居之則不當位而凶亦可辯其為非是則非中之
四爻不能備也噫論卦則一言而有餘論爻則累言
而不足聖人贊易之意何其至歟抑論之易之所有
者卦卦之所有者爻卦具夫爻而爻即所以為卦者
也易書具夫卦爻而卦爻即所以為易者也易之未
作卦爻在造化易之既作造化在卦爻然則卦爻者

… it contains hexagrams, and it contains lines. Speaking in terms of the hexagrams, one must trace the beginning of an affair and summarize its end. Once the beginning and end of the affair are both present, the substance and nature of the hexagram are already formed; this is why a hexagram has a fixed substance. Speaking in terms of the lines, the nine [yang] and six [yin] are used in alternation, and the firm and yielding dwell intermingled. Because their times and positions differ, the objects they take as symbols also vary; this is why the lines have no fixed function. Such is the way the Sage spoke of the substance and function of the hexagrams and lines.

Furthermore, speaking in terms of the first and topmost lines: the first line is the root of the hexagram, and as the root, its nature is not yet manifest, so it is difficult to know; the topmost line is the tip of the hexagram, and as the tip, its nature is already evident, so it is easy to know. Because it is difficult to know, the words appended to it can only be obtained after deliberation and discussion; because it is easy to know, one simply concludes the words and completes the end of the hexagram. Thus these first and topmost lines constitute another principle of the Changes (Yi).

Speaking further in terms of the four middle lines: for instance, with Zhen below and Kan above, the hexagram form is Zhun [Difficulty at the Beginning]. If we reckon its intermingled lines, from the second to the fourth line is the overlapping trigram Kun, whose symbolic object is earth and which possesses the virtue of docility; from the third to the fifth line is the overlapping trigram Gen, whose symbolic object is mountain and which possesses the virtue of stopping. The fifth place is a yang position, and when occupied by a yang line, it matches the position and is auspicious, so one can certainly discern that it is right; the second place is a yin position, and if occupied by a yang line, it does not match the position and is inauspicious, so one can also discern that it is wrong. Such things cannot be fully provided for except by the four middle lines.

Alas! In discussing the hexagrams, a single statement is more than enough; in discussing the lines, repeated statements are still not sufficient. How consummately thorough was the Sage's intention in praising the Changes! Yet if we discuss it further, what the Changes possesses are hexagrams, and what the hexagrams possess are lines. A hexagram comprises the lines, and the lines are themselves what make up the hexagram; the Book of Changes comprises the hexagrams and lines, and the hexagrams and lines are themselves what make up the Changes. Before the Changes was made, the hexagrams and lines resided in the creative transformations of nature; once the Changes was made, the creative transformations of nature resided in the hexagrams and lines. Thus the hexagrams and lines…

…are they not the deep reserves of the creative transformation of nature? Are they not the very essence of the Sages?

Book of Documents (Shu): "They are called rain, clearing, obscurity, disconnection, and crossing."

Associate Examiner Vice Director Shen comments: This topic speaks exclusively of tortoise-shell divination cracks, yet most writers muddle it together with yarrow-stalk hexagram divination, leaving the reader frustrated. This essay is concise in diction and clear in reasoning, without losing the essential meaning of the text—how could a high recommendation be undeserved!
Associate Examiner Erudite Xu comments: It grasps the essential meaning deeply; worthy of selection.
Associate Examiner Senior Compiler Yue comments: The topic is inherently plain, and most writers found themselves hard-pressed, yet this piece elucidates it deeply; therefore I have selected it.
Examiner Expositor-in-waiting Lü comments: Its elucidation of the divination cracks is something no other paper reached.
Examiner Academician Xue comments: Concise in words and thorough in meaning; the concluding section is especially lofty.

The noble man sets forth the categories of tortoise-shell divination in order to make manifest the cracks of divination. Now, wherever there is tortoise-shell divination there must be cracks, and those cracks refer precisely to the Five Phases. How could the noble man who elucidates the Nine Categories not list their headings and clarify their cracks? In antiquity, when Viscount of Ji (Jizi) expounded the category of "Examination of Doubts" and touched upon this, his meaning was that when the state has great affairs, it cannot be without doubts, and the resolution of doubts must rely upon tortoise-shell divination. For tortoise-shell divination is that whereby one scorches the tortoise shell and observes the cracks so as to determine good and ill fortune. Therefore, at a single scorching for a tortoise-shell crack, there is that which is called "rain." That it is named "rain" must be because the ink absorbed by the crack is moist and glossy like rain; and as a crack, "rain" among the Five Phases…

title: 天順元年會試錄
text:
則為水也有曰霽者焉名之以霽者必其所食之墨
光明而開霽霽之為兆在五行則為火也其曰蒙者
蒙昧不明也而蒙昧不明其兆非五行之木乎其曰
驛者絡驛不屬也而絡驛不屬其兆非五行之金乎
至若交錯有相勝之意者謂之克克之為兆又所以
為五行之土也是則因所卜雨霽蒙驛克之目而著
水火木金土之兆由是推衍以極其變於無窮則天
下之疑又焉有不决者哉抑考稽疑之疇以卜筮為
主此既言龜之卜下文曰貞曰悔又言蓍之占至於
===
君及卿士庶人龜筮從違則專以卜筮為重雖曰古
者大事卜小事筮謂之筮短龜長然夫子贊易有曰
探賾索隱鈞深致遠以定天下之吉凶成天下之亹
亹者莫大乎蓍龜則筮龜者又豈非萬世决疑之大
法也歟
拜手稽首后矣曰宅乃事宅乃牧宅乃準兹惟
后矣謀面用丕訓德則乃宅人兹乃三宅無義
民

則為水也。有曰霽者焉，名之以霽者，必其所食之墨光明而開霽，霽之為兆，在五行則為火也。其曰蒙者，蒙昧不明也；而蒙昧不明，其兆非五行之木乎？其曰驛者，絡驛不屬也；而絡驛不屬，其兆非五行之金乎？至若交錯有相勝之意者，謂之克，克之為兆，又所以為五行之土也。是則因所卜雨、霽、蒙、驛、克之目，而著水、火、木、金、土之兆，由是推衍以極其變於無窮，則天下之疑又焉有不决者哉？抑考稽疑之疇，以卜筮為主。此既言龜之卜，下文「曰貞、曰悔」又言蓍之占，至於君及卿士、庶人、龜筮從違，則專以卜筮為重。雖曰古者大事卜、小事筮，謂之「筮短龜長」，然夫子贊《易》有曰：「探賾索隱，鈞深致遠，以定天下之吉凶，成天下之亹亹者，莫大乎蓍龜。」則筮龜者，又豈非萬世决疑之大法也歟？

translation_en:
… corresponds to Water. There is that called "clearing" (ji); to name it "clearing" means that the ink absorbed by the crack must be bright and clear like an opening sky, and as an omen, "clearing" among the Five Phases corresponds to Fire. That which is called "obscurity" (meng) means gloomy and indistinct; and being gloomy and indistinct, is its omen not Wood among the Five Phases? That which is called "intermittence" (yi) means sparse and discontinuous; and being sparse and discontinuous, is its omen not Metal among the Five Phases? As for cracks that intersect with the sense of overcoming one another, this is called "crossing" (ke), and as an omen, "crossing" is what corresponds to Earth among the Five Phases. Thus, based on the divination categories of rain, clearing, obscurity, intermittence, and crossing, the omens of Water, Fire, Wood, Metal, and Earth are made manifest. By extending and deducing from these to exhaust their infinite variations, how could there be any doubts under heaven that remain unresolved? Furthermore, if we examine the category of "Examination of Doubts" (Jiyi), it takes tortoise-shell and milfoil divination as its foundation. Here it has already spoken of divination by the tortoise shell; the text below—"called the inner hexagram (zhen), called the outer hexagram (hui)"—goes on to speak of divination by milfoil stalks; and when it comes to the agreement or disagreement among the ruler, the ministers and officers, the common people, the tortoise shell, and the milfoil stalks, great weight is placed specifically upon tortoise-shell and milfoil divination. Although it was said that in antiquity great matters were divined by tortoise shell and small matters by milfoil, referred to as "milfoil is inferior and the tortoise shell superior," yet when the Master praised the Book of Changes (Yi), he said: "To explore what is complex and search out what is hidden, to hook up what is deep and reach what is distant, thereby determining good and bad fortune in the world and accomplishing the tireless endeavors of the world, nothing is greater than milfoil and the tortoise shell." Are not milfoil and tortoise-shell divination, then, the great standard for resolving doubts for ten thousand generations?

"I bow my head to my hands and to the ground before the Sovereign, saying: 'Establish your managers of affairs, establish your pastors, establish your guardians of the law; in this way you are truly the Sovereign. If by judging merely from appearances you take them to be of great and compliant virtue, and on that basis appoint men to office, then these three high positions will be devoid of righteous men.'"

text:

容當時告君氣象殆盡必是作手高薦何疑

章㫖可取
同考試官脩撰岳批作者多不識題意所以講

考試官侍講呂批體認經意而形之為文反覆詳
盡超於衆作遠矣
考試官學士薛批此題先尊其為君之名中叙
===
其為君之實末以輕於用人為告作者多失
倫次惟是篇發明三節之意詳盡必深於壁
經者也
古人致敬以告君必言審於用人則有以盡其實輕
於用人則無以得乎賢夫審於用人者為君之實也
苟非迪知忱恂之審而輕於謀面以用人則三宅又
豈復有賢者乎在昔有夏大臣既迪知忱恂于九德
之行必拜手稽首以告其君若曰端拱五位人君之
名尊之極矣必有以副其所以尊君臨萬邦人君之

Comment by Associate Examiner Vice Director Shen: This topic is inherently difficult to handle, yet this composition almost completely captures the spirit of advising the ruler at that time. He must be a skilled writer; what doubt can there be about recommending him highly!

Comment by Associate Examiner Archivist Xu: All seven essays are complete in both expression and principle, and this one in particular deeply grasps the purport of the passage. It is worthy of selection.

Comment by Associate Examiner Senior Compiler Yue: Most writers do not understand the meaning of the topic, and therefore their exposition and synthesis are unclear. This essay grasps it and truly deserves high advancement.

Comment by Examiner Expositor-in-waiting Lü: He personally realizes the meaning of the Classic and gives it form in writing, repeatedly and exhaustively, surpassing the multitude of other compositions by far.

Comment by Examiner Academician Xue: This topic first honors the name of being a ruler, in the middle recounts the reality of being a ruler, and at the end offers counsel against taking the employment of men lightly. Most writers lose the proper sequence; only this essay elucidates the meaning of the three sections exhaustively. He must be someone deeply versed in the Wall Classic [the Book of Documents].

When the ancients showed utmost respect in advising their ruler, they necessarily said that being careful in employing men provides the means to fulfill the reality of rulership, whereas being careless in employing men leaves one with no means to obtain the worthy. Now, being careful in employing men is the reality of being a ruler. If one does not have the carefulness of truly knowing and sincerely trusting them, and instead carelessly relies on mere appearances in employing men, then how could there ever again be worthy men in the three appointed positions? translation_en:
…positions are the heads of the hundred offices and the mainstay in establishing governance. If the three positions [are filled by the right?] men, then when the headrope is lifted the meshes open, and the governance of all under Heaven is thereby established. This, moreover, is the profound intent of the Duke of Zhou, which the reader must not fail to understand.

Classic of Poetry (Shi)
"The great target is set up; the bows and arrows are strung and readied. The archers are matched in pairs; present yourfeats of shooting! Shoot at that mark, to pray for your cup [to spare yourself the penalty draught]. With flute dances, mouth-organs, and drums, the music is harmoniously performed; we offer unto and delight our illustrious ancestors, to consummate the hundred rites. When the hundred rites have all been performed, grand and abundant are they; they bestow upon you pure blessings." [Ode 220, "Bin zhi chu yan"]
He Yin
Associate Examiner and Acting Director (shu langzhong) Weng comments: The explanation of principles is precise and detailed, and the phrasing is gentle and generous. None without a deep mastery of the Classic of Poetry (Pajing) could expound it to this degree; it ought to be selected for publication.
Associate Examiner and Reader-in-Waiting (shidu) Sun comments: This essay shows genuine and earnest comprehension, and its style is concise and fitting. Reading it is like "one leading the chant and three joining in with sighs," leaving a lingering resonance. Truly admirable, truly admirable!
Associate Examiner and Vice Minister (shaoqing) Qian comments: In discussing how in archery one seeks to compete for victory whereas in sacrifice one must receive blessings [?], the language is incisive and the reasoning clear. He is truly adept at explaining the Odes.
Examiner and Expositor-in-Waiting (shijiang) Lü comments: The diction and tone are calm and dignified, superior to the crowd of compositions.
Examiner and Academician (xueshi) Xue comments: The reasoning is clear and the words are not unfocused; in particular, it succeeds in drawing out at the conclusion the substance of self-cultivation and advancement among military men [or: the men of King Wu]. An excellent piece.

title: 天順元年會試錄
text:
其福盖射必先乎器備耦齊而祭必本乎樂和禮盛
也苟非器耦之齊備固不足以行射而非禮樂之和
盛又何以奉祭而獲福哉且夫射有器焉有耦焉以
器言則大侯者君侯也今而既抗則非掩束之際弓
矢者射器也今而斯張則非弨兮之時然器已備矣
而耦不齊可乎由是選次其才而三耦無不比簡擇
其人而衆耦無不同斯時也獻爾發功各心競云吾
必四鍭如樹以求爵于爾焉發彼有的以祈爵于女
焉茲非器備耦齊而行射者較其能乎若夫祭有樂
===
焉有禮焉以樂言則籥舞者文舞也今而秉籥舞蹈
與笙鼓之相應烈祖者有功之祖也今而樂聲和奏
致烈祖之懽悅然樂已和矣而禮不備又可乎由是
以洽百禮而無一禮之不至有壬有林而無一禮之
不備斯時也烈祖有靈來格來享必於冥冥之中而
錫爾以盛福焉昭昭之頃而降爾以純嘏焉茲非樂
和禮盛而主祭者獲其福乎抑是詩衛武公飲酒悔
過而作也不特此耳考之國語在輿有旅賁之規位
宁有官師之典以至倚几居寢之有箴臨事宴居之

… his blessings. For archery must first have the implements prepared and the pairs matched, while sacrifice must be rooted in the music being harmonious and the rites grand. If the implements and pairs are not matched and prepared, it is certainly insufficient to perform the archery ritual; and if the rites and music are not harmonious and grand, how then could one offer the sacrifice and obtain blessings?

Moreover, in archery there are implements and there are pairs. Speaking in terms of the implements: the great target is the ruler's target; now that it is already set up on high, it is no longer the moment when it lies furled and bound. The bows and arrows are the implements of archery; now that they are strung, it is no longer the time when they are unstrung and slack. Yet once the implements are prepared, would it do for the pairs not to be matched? Thereupon, they select and rank their talents so that the three pairs are all well matched, and they choose the men so that the many pairs are all in accord. At this time, "displaying your skill in shooting," each competes in his heart, saying: "I shall surely plant my four arrows as if set in a stand, so as to seek the penalty cup from you; I shall shoot at that mark, so as to pray for the penalty cup for you!" Is this not a case of the implements being prepared and the pairs matched, while those who perform the archery ritual compete in their skill?

As for the sacrifice, there is music and there are rites. Speaking in terms of the music: the flute dance is the civil dance; now, holding the flutes, they dance and tread in response to the reed organs and drums. The Illustrious Ancestor is the ancestor of merit; now, the musical notes are harmoniously played, bringing joy to the Illustrious Ancestor. Yet once the music is harmonious, would it do for the rites not to be complete? Thereupon, "to consummate the hundred rites," there is not a single rite that is not carried to perfection; "grandly and fully," there is not a single rite that is not complete. At this time, the Illustrious Ancestor in his numinous spirit comes to approach and comes to enjoy the offering; surely from the unseen realm he will bestow upon you abundant blessings, and in the bright daylight he will send down upon you pure felicity. Is this not a case of the music being harmonious and the rites grand, while he who presides over the sacrifice obtains his blessings?

title: 天順元年會試錄
text:
周人於郊祀得不尊之以配天哉思昔周人意若曰
生民者天也養民者稷也今我有事南郊之時陶匏
既具藁秸既陳斯時也欲尊太王以配天而太王克
勤王家而已求其真可配天者非我文德之后稷乎
欲尊文王以配天而文王已配明堂矣求其真可配
天者惟我文德之后稷焉然其德之所以配天果何
以見之哉當夫洪水滔天之日黎民阻饑百姓艱食
斯時也契雖敷五教然民食不足則五教不興稷則
教民稼穡使人得以粒食者莫非其德之至也禹雖
奠民居然民食不充則居止弗康稷則播時百穀俾
民得以無饑者又非其德之至乎噫后稷養民之德
如此其至是宜尊之以配天也歟大抵此郊祀獻后
稷之樂歌也及觀生民之詩尊稷配天而作其辭詳
此亦尊稷配天而作其辭簡何哉盖彼為叙事宜詳
不詳無以見其始終此為郊祀宜簡不簡無以著其
嚴肅此雅頌之所以别也
春秋

punctuated:
周人於郊祀，得不尊之以配天哉？思昔周人意若曰：「生民者，天也；養民者，稷也。今我有事南郊之時，陶匏既具，藁秸既陳。斯時也，欲尊太王以配天，而太王克勤王家而已，求其真可配天者，非我文德之后稷乎？欲尊文王以配天，而文王已配明堂矣，求其真可配天者，惟我文德之后稷焉。」然其德之所以配天，果何以見之哉？當夫洪水滔天之日，黎民阻饑，百姓艱食。斯時也，契雖敷五教，然民食不足，則五教不興；稷則教民稼穡，使人得以粒食者，莫非其德之至也。禹雖奠民居，然民食不充，則居止弗康；稷則播時百穀，俾民得以無饑者，又非其德之至乎？噫！后稷養民之德如此其至，是宜尊之以配天也歟！大抵此郊祀獻后稷之樂歌也。及觀《生民》之詩，尊稷配天而作，其辭詳；此亦尊稷配天而作，其辭簡。何哉？盖彼為叙事，宜詳，不詳無以見其始終；此為郊祀，宜簡，不簡無以著其嚴肅。此雅、頌之所以别也。
春秋
公會齊侯、宋公、陳侯、鄭伯同盟于幽。〔莊公二十七年〕
translation_en:
…how could the people of Zhou, in their suburban sacrifice, not honor him as the correlate of Heaven? Thinking back to the people of Zhou in antiquity, their intention was as if to say: "It is Heaven that gives birth to the people; it is Houji (Lord Millet) who nourishes the people. Now, when we perform the sacrifice at the southern suburb, the earthenware and gourd vessels are prepared, and the straw mats are spread out. At this moment, should we wish to honor King Tai as the correlate of Heaven, King Tai merely labored diligently for the royal house; if we seek one who can truly be the correlate of Heaven, is it not our Houji of civil virtue? Should we wish to honor King Wen as the correlate of Heaven, King Wen is already the correlate in the Hall of Light (Mingtang); if we seek one who can truly be the correlate of Heaven, there is only our Houji of civil virtue." Yet by what means can it truly be seen that his virtue qualifies him to be the correlate of Heaven? In the days when the floodwaters swelled to Heaven, the black-haired people suffered from famine and the hundred surnames struggled to find food. At that time, although Xie propagated the Five Teachings, if the people's food was insufficient, the Five Teachings could not flourish; Houji, however, taught the people to sow and reap, enabling everyone to eat grain—none of this was anything less than the utmost of his virtue. Although Yu settled the people's dwellings, if the people's food was not abundant, their settlements could not be at peace; Houji, however, sowed the hundred grains in season, enabling the people to be free from hunger—was this too not the utmost of his virtue? Ah! Since Houji's virtue in nourishing the people reached such an ultimate degree, is it not fitting to honor him as the correlate of Heaven! Broadly speaking, this is the musical song offered to Houji at the suburban sacrifice. Yet when we look at the ode "Shengmin" (The Birth of Our People), which was composed to honor Houji as the correlate of Heaven, its words are detailed; whereas this ode, which was also composed to honor Houji as the correlate of Heaven, is concise in its words. Why is this? Because that ode is a narrative, so it ought to be detailed—without detail there is no way to show the story from beginning to end; whereas this ode is for the suburban sacrifice, so it ought to be concise—without conciseness there is no way to manifest its solemnity and reverence. This is the distinction between the Daya (Greater Odes) and the Song (Hymns).

鄭伯亦悔于厥心而乞盟焉夫鄭素以叛服靡常之
國而始終從齊如此則天下人心孰有不從者乎由
是葵丘載盟衣裳咸集森然五禁之嚴巋然一王之
重諸侯咸喻其志矣夫諸侯之喻伯功之盛也迹其所以
伯功之盛非由得鄭而何迨晋自平丘同盟以終無
復糾合為心鄭其有窺於此是以首會于鹹謀貳晋
===
也既推齊侯以同好盟于曲濮謀從齊也復偕衛侯
以結言無何齊景之圖伯日勤安甫之載書復設游
速又銜君命以從事焉夫鄭世以懿親同姓之邦而
先後貳晋如此則天下諸侯其有不貳者乎巳而黄
池有會夫差寔臨乃以姬姓之長率先晋魯之盟夷
勢亦巳盛矣夫夷勢之盛伯政之分也泝其所以伯
政之分非由失鄭而何吁原一鄭從違之殊見二伯
盛衰之判比事以觀而春秋始終見矣雖然先乎盟
幽以抗周固鄭也後乎葵丘以朝楚亦鄭也則何恠

punctuated:
日以尊安為事，鄭其有契於此。是以于幽同盟，尊王室也，既委弁冕而在列；𡩋母有盟，通王貢也，復遣子華以聽命。未幾，王人之告難踵来，于洮之盟事復講，鄭伯亦悔于厥心而乞盟焉。夫鄭素以叛服靡常之國，而始終從齊如此，則天下人心孰有不從者乎？由是葵丘載盟，衣裳咸集，森然五禁之嚴，巋然一王之重，諸侯咸喻其志矣。夫諸侯之喻，伯功之盛也；迹其所以伯功之盛，非由得鄭而何？

迨晋自平丘同盟以終，無復糾合為心，鄭其有窺於此。是以首會于鹹，謀貳晋也，既推齊侯以同好；盟于曲濮，謀從齊也，復偕衛侯以結言。無何，齊景之圖伯日勤，安甫之載書復設，游速又銜君命以從事焉。夫鄭世以懿親同姓之邦，而先後貳晋如此，則天下諸侯其有不貳者乎？巳而黄池有會，夫差寔臨，乃以姬姓之長，率先晋魯之盟，夷勢亦巳盛矣。夫夷勢之盛，伯政之分也；泝其所以伯政之分，非由失鄭而何？

吁！原一鄭從違之殊，見二伯盛衰之判，比事以觀，而《春秋》始終見矣。雖然，先乎盟幽以抗周，固鄭也；後乎葵丘以朝楚，亦鄭也。則何恠
translation_en:
…daily made honoring the royal house and pacifying the realm its business, and Zheng surely felt an affinity with this. Therefore, in the joint covenant at You, which was to honor the royal house, [the ruler of Zheng] appeared in ceremonial cap and robes to take his place in the ranks; and when there was a covenant at Ningmu, which was to ensure the flow of royal tribute, he again dispatched Zihua to receive commands. Before long, the King's men arrived on one another's heels to report crises, and when the covenant at Tao was once again negotiated, the Earl of Zheng also repented in his heart and begged to join the covenant. Now, since Zheng was a state habitually known for its inconstant rebellion and submission, yet followed Qi from beginning to end like this, whose heart in the realm would not follow? Consequently, when the covenant at Kuiqiu was concluded, the princes all gathered in robes and skirts [of peace]; with the solemnity of the five prohibitions and the towering weight of the one King, the feudal lords all understood [Duke Huan of Qi's] intent. That the feudal lords understood his intent marked the zenith of hegemonic achievement; tracing the reason for the zenith of this hegemonic achievement, what else did it stem from if not winning over Zheng?

When it came to Jin, from the end of the joint covenant at Pingqiu onward, it no longer had its heart set on uniting the lords, and Zheng surely saw through this. Therefore, it first met at Xian, plotting to become duplicitous toward Jin, and promoted the Marquis of Qi in shared friendship; it covenanted at Qupu, plotting to follow Qi, and joined the Marquis of Wei in pledging words. Before long, Duke Jing of Qi grew daily more diligent in his designs for hegemony, and when the covenant text at Anfu was again drawn up, You Su once more carried his ruler's command to participate in the affair. Now, since Zheng was for generations a state of close royal kinship sharing the same surname [as Jin], yet repeatedly became duplicitous toward Jin like this, among the feudal lords of the realm who would not become duplicitous? Soon thereafter, there was the meeting at Huangchi, where Fuchai [of Wu] appeared in person, and claiming precedence among the states of the Ji surname, he led the covenant ahead of Jin and Lu—the power of the barbarians had indeed become formidable! The formidable power of the barbarians marked the division of hegemonic authority; tracing back the reason for the division of hegemonic authority, what else did it stem from if not losing Zheng?

Alas! By examining the difference between the compliance and defiance of this single state of Zheng, one sees the distinction between the rise and decline of the two hegemons; when we place the events side by side to observe them, the beginning and end of the Spring and Autumn Annals are revealed. Even so, prior to the covenant at You, it was indeed Zheng that defied Zhou; and subsequent to Kuiqiu, it was also Zheng that paid court to Chu. Then what wonder is it…

translation_en:
… that at the end of the Spring and Autumn period it abandoned Jin to follow Qi! Therefore, observing the beginning and end of this single state of Zheng causes us concern not only for the royal house, but also for the hegemonic enterprise; and not only for the hegemonic enterprise, but for the state of the world. Alas!

"The people of Qi invaded our northern border" [26th year of Duke Xi]; "The people of Jin and the people of Qin besieged Zheng" [30th year of Duke Xi]; "The Duke met the Marquis of Qi at Jiagu" [10th year of Duke Ding]; "The Duke met the Marquis of Wei and Huang Yuan of Song at Yun" [12th year of Duke Ai].
By Zuo Zan.
Comment by Associate Examiner and Secretary (zhushi) Zhu: [Since the topic is based on the Zuo Tradition (Zuozhuan), it is not difficult to phrase a response, yet candidates uniformly offer praise, which hardly seems the ultimate judgment. This essay apportions praise and critique aptly, and at the close returns to honoring Confucius; the author must be a scholar of discernment and deserves to be placed high among the selections.]
Comment by Associate Examiner and Vice Minister (shaoqing) Qian: [When comparing people, one must compare those of the same category—how can one compare a sage like Confucius with the other three men? At the end, this composition alone places supreme weight on Confucius and laments that the rulers of the time could not make full use of him, thereby grasping the essential meaning.]
Comment by Examiner and Expositor-in-waiting (shijiang) Lü: [On the matters of repelling armies and moving men, this essay cites evidence clearly and weighs them with due proportion; it is truly a fine piece.]
Comment by Examiner and Academician (xueshi) Xue: [In distinguishing between righteousness and profit, and between achievement and moral transformation, it deeply grasps the import of strictness and rigor.]

Repelling an army through righteousness is certainly superior to repelling it through…

title: 天順元年會試錄
text:
以言此可見魯鄭退師有義利之辨而二賢感人有
功化之異也嗟夫齊孝以洮向二盟致憾於魯遂興
夫北鄙之伐晉文以出亡不禮宿怨於鄭是以有圍
鄭之師斯時也魯則室如縣罄鄭則秦晉合攻二國
亦云殆矣幸而展喜犒師受命展禽舉先王盟府之
言陳棄命廢職之語齊遂悅於義而班師之恐後燭
之武夜入秦師啓以鄰厚君薄之故誘以闕秦利晉
之言秦則悅於利而退焉假曰以利紓患愈於待斃
比之陳大義以卻之何如春秋所以特嚴於義利之
===
辨者此也至若齊景以我師再侵欲駕乎魯相率為
夾谷之會夫差以行人之故欲報乎衛於是有會鄫
之行是時也齊則萊夷之兵遽起吳則藩舍之謀已
見二君亦幾危矣時而孔子相禮歷階而升卻其裔
夷之俘示以德義之正齊遂感於禮而謝過之不暇
子貢往見宰嚭喻以墮黨崇讎之失動夫難以為伯
之言吳則感其言而釋焉借曰片言存衛賢於用兵
比之孚神化以感之又何如春秋所以特著夫功化
之異者此也雖然燭之武之卻敵固不可與展禽而

punctuated: 以言。此可見魯、鄭退師有義、利之辨，而二賢感人有功、化之異也。嗟夫！齊孝以洮、向二盟致憾於魯，遂興夫北鄙之伐；晉文以出亡不禮宿怨於鄭，是以有圍鄭之師。斯時也，魯則室如縣罄，鄭則秦、晉合攻，二國亦云殆矣。幸而展喜犒師，受命展禽，舉先王盟府之言，陳棄命廢職之語，齊遂悅於義而班師之恐後；燭之武夜入秦師，啓以鄰厚君薄之故，誘以闕秦利晉之言，秦則悅於利而退焉。假曰以利紓患，愈於待斃，比之陳大義以卻之，何如？《春秋》所以特嚴於義、利之辨者，此也。至若齊景以我師再侵，欲駕乎魯，相率為夾谷之會；夫差以行人之故，欲報乎衛，於是有會鄫之行。是時也，齊則萊夷之兵遽起，吳則藩舍之謀已見，二君亦幾危矣。時而孔子相禮，歷階而升，卻其裔夷之俘，示以德義之正，齊遂感於禮而謝過之不暇；子貢往見宰嚭，喻以墮黨崇讎之失，動夫難以為伯之言，吳則感其言而釋焉。借曰片言存衛，賢於用兵，比之孚神化以感之，又何如？《春秋》所以特著夫功、化之異者，此也。雖然，燭之武之卻敵，固不可與展禽而
translation_en:
… through speech. From this one can see that between Lu and Zheng repelling enemy armies there is the distinction between righteousness and profit, and between the two worthies moving people there is the difference between mere achievement and transformative influence.

Alas! Because of the two covenants at Tao and Xiang, Duke Xiao of Qi (Qi Xiao 齊孝) harbored resentment toward Lu and consequently launched a punitive expedition against its northern frontier; because of the old grievance that he had not been treated with propriety while in exile, Duke Wen of Jin (Jin Wen 晉文) harbored rancor toward Zheng, and therefore there was the army that besieged Zheng. At that time, Lu's houses were as empty as hanging musical stones, while Zheng faced the combined attack of Qin and Jin; the two states could indeed be called imperiled! Fortunately, when Zhan Xi 展喜 went to reward the troops with provisions, he received his instructions from Zhan Qin 展禽, citing the words of the former kings preserved in the repository of covenants and setting forth arguments about abandoning mandates and neglecting duties; Qi was thereupon pleased by righteousness and withdrew its army as if fearing to be late. Zhu Zhiwu 燭之武 entered the Qin camp at night, explaining the reason why strengthening one's neighbor weakens oneself, and enticing them with talk of diminishing Qin to benefit Jin; Qin was thereupon pleased by profit and retreated. Even supposing one says that relieving disaster through profit is better than waiting for destruction, how does that compare with setting forth great righteousness to repel them? This is why the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) is especially strict regarding the distinction between righteousness and profit.

As for Duke Jing of Qi (Qi Jing 齊景), because our troops had twice invaded, he wished to gain superiority over Lu, and so they met together at the assembly of Jiagu 夾谷; Fuchai 夫差, on account of the envoy, wished to retaliate against Wei, and consequently there was the expedition to the meeting at Zeng 鄫. At that time, on Qi's side the troops of the Lai barbarians (Lai Yi 萊夷) suddenly rose up, while on Wu's side the plot to fence in the ruler's lodgings had already appeared; both rulers were nearly in peril. Timely then did Confucius (Kongzi 孔子) assist in the ceremonial rites: striding up the steps, he repulsed those captives from the frontier barbarians and showed them the correctness of moral virtue and righteousness, whereupon Qi was moved by ritual propriety and had scarcely time enough to apologize for its fault. Zigong 子貢 went to see Grand宰 Pi (Zai Pi 宰嚭), making him understand the error of destroying allies and exalting enemies, and stirring him with the argument that it would be difficult by such means to become hegemon, whereupon Wu was moved by his words and released [the ruler of Wei]. Even granting that preserving Wei with a few words is superior to using military force, how again does that compare with inspiring others through the sincerity of spiritual transformation? This is why the Spring and Autumn Annals makes especially manifest the difference between achievement and transformative influence.

Even so, although Zhu Zhiwu's repelling of the enemy certainly cannot be [compared on equal terms] with Zhan Qin…

text:
如此人君可不誕敷仁政以順生道之宣泄乎何則
天為萬物之父母而運其時人君為萬民之父母而
施其政是故凡物塞於冬而通於春始於子而極於
午時至季春之月生育之氣方盛非若仲夏之極盛
也陽和之氣發泄非如仲冬之閉塞也然氣運於無
形物生於有象由是向之曲生而未拆者今則乘化
工之機而畢出無一物之不遂其生昔之直生而未
伸者今則感陽和之氣而盡達無一類之不順其性
曰方盛曰發泄生道之宣泄如此君人者當體天以
===

punctuated: 如此，人君可不誕敷仁政，以順生道之宣泄乎？何則？天為萬物之父母而運其時，人君為萬民之父母而施其政。是故凡物塞於冬而通於春，始於子而極於午。時至季春之月，生育之氣方盛，非若仲夏之極盛也；陽和之氣發泄，非如仲冬之閉塞也。然氣運於無形，物生於有象。由是向之曲生而未拆者，今則乘化工之機而畢出，無一物之不遂其生；昔之直生而未伸者，今則感陽和之氣而盡達，無一類之不順其性。曰「方盛」、曰「發泄」，生道之宣泄如此，君人者當體天以行政，不可內而不出也，若內而不出，則違夫時矣；曰「畢出」、曰「盡達」，萬物之化生若彼，長民者當順時以施仁，不宜吝嗇閉藏也，苟吝嗇閉藏，則逆其令矣。于以布其德澤，施其恩惠：在內則命有司發倉廩以賜貧窮，開府庫以周天下，使德澤之覃被，同一天地之發生也；在外則命諸侯厚幣帛以聘名士，致尊敬以禮賢者，俾恩惠之溥施，均一雨露之沾濡也。吁！人君布德行惠以施仁政，其體天子民之意為何如哉！雖然，此既曰「不可以內」，至於季秋又曰「無有宣出」，何也？蓋

Heaven acts as the father and mother of the myriad things and revolves its seasons; the ruler of men acts as the father and mother of the myriad people and dispenses his governance. Therefore, all things are blocked up in winter and opened through in spring, beginning at the zi month and reaching their culmination in the wu month. When the season reaches the last month of spring, the vital force of generation and growth is just coming into its fullness—unlike in mid-summer, when it reaches its utmost fullness; the vital force of warm yang is venting and pouring forth—unlike in mid-winter, when it is closed and blocked up. Now, vital force revolves in the formless, while things are born into visible form. Consequently, those sprouts that previously grew bent and had not yet split open now ride the mechanism of creative transformation and come forth completely, with not a single thing failing to fulfill its life; those shoots that formerly grew straight and had not yet stretched out are now stirred by the vital force of warm yang and reach full development, with not a single kind failing to follow its nature. In saying "just coming into its fullness" and "venting and pouring forth," such is the burgeoning forth of the Way of life; he who rules over men ought to embody Heaven in carrying out governance and must not take in without giving out—for if he takes in without giving out, he violates the season. In saying "come forth completely" and "reach full development," such is the transformative generation of the myriad things; he who presides over the people ought to accord with the season in dispensing benevolence and should not be stingy or hoard away—for if he is stingy and hoards away, he goes against its ordinance. Thereby he spreads his virtuous bounty and dispenses his gracious favor: within the court, he orders the authorities to open the granaries to bestow grain upon the poor and destitute, and to open the treasuries to succor the realm, causing the far-reaching cover of his virtuous bounty to be one and the same as the generative emergence of Heaven and Earth; outside in the domains, he orders the feudal lords to make generous gifts of silk to invite men of renown, and to show utmost respect in treating the worthy with ritual courtesy, causing the universal dispensation of his gracious favor to be equal to the moistening saturation of rain and dew. Ah! When the ruler of men spreads virtue and practices kindness so as to dispense benevolent governance, how profound is his intention to embody Heaven and treat the people as his children! text:
春為天德之元而陽氣為之發舒故季春之令
則曰不可以內所以順夫陽也秋為天德之利
而陰氣為之肅斂故季秋之令則曰無有宣出所以
順夫陰也此人君施斂之政無非順陰陽之義也歟
故曰聖人與天地合其德
取數多者仁也夫勉於仁者不亦難乎是故君
子以義度人則難為人以人望人則賢者可知

子比干迹雖不同而名為仁則同然特仁之一事耳

之取數多也可知以其取數之多故雖終日乾乾盡

translation_en:
…the source of all goodness. How can we see that benevolence embraces so many aspects? Guan Zhong, Weizi, Jizi, and Bi Gan differed in their deeds, yet were alike in being called benevolent. Nevertheless, these were merely individual instances of benevolence. Warmth, goodness, respect, circumspection, generosity, forbearance, humility, and courtesy differ in their application, yet share a common basis in benevolence. Nevertheless, these are merely particular aspects of benevolence. If we speak of its fullness, even sages have things they cannot accomplish; if we extend benevolence to its utmost reach, even Yao and Shun would find it difficult. Thus we can see—and can know—that benevolence embraces many aspects [the wording here appears disordered and repetitive: ?]. Because it embraces so many aspects, even those who strive tirelessly all day and devote their whole hearts to practising it cannot bear its burden. This is what is meant by “Those who lift it cannot sustain it.” Though they apply themselves diligently every day and exhaust their strength in seeking it, they cannot readily attain its realm. This is what is meant by “Those who travel its path cannot reach its end.” Is it not difficult, then, to strive for benevolence?

Precisely because the way of benevolence is so difficult, if a gentleman measures others by the full demands of righteousness, expecting their strengths and weaknesses, their greater and lesser capacities, all to be appropriate, and the relative weight of their qualities to be fitting, then only someone who embodies it completely and without interruption can meet that standard. Yet throughout the world there is no perfect person. Hence the saying, “Then it is difficult to be a person.” If we compare people today with one another, the greatly worthy surpass the less worthy, and those with six virtues excel those with three. This is what is meant by “There are indeed those who are better than others.” One does not, however, demand perfection of others. Hence the saying, “Then the worthy can be recognized.”

Ah! There are many ways of practising benevolence, and those who strive for it find achievement difficult. Benevolence differs from person to person, and those who acknowledge it in others do not demand perfection. The sage spoke these words, and the recorder set them down in the “Record of Exemplary Conduct” (Biao ji). Is not their intended instruction profoundly significant? The author must be a scholar who has long immersed his mind in fundamental learning; reading it three times over inspires reverence.

The discourse reads: The sage has the wherewithal to keep whole the virtues of activity and tranquility, and in his activity he always takes tranquility as its foundation. For the Way of the Supreme Ultimate (Taiji) is present everywhere, yet only the sage has the wherewithal to keep it whole. Why is this? Equilibrium and humanity are the virtues of his activity, and they are none other than the Supreme Ultimate in activity as yang; correctness and righteousness are the virtues of his tranquility, and they are none other than the Supreme Ultimate in tranquility as yin. Since the sage has the wherewithal to keep whole these virtues of equilibrium, correctness, humanity, and righteousness—of activity and tranquility—and since that which is active always takes that which is tranquil as its foundation, then in his activity, where does he go that is not equilibrium and humanity, and how could equilibrium and humanity ever fail to be the doing of correctness and righteousness, which belong to tranquility? Allow me to elaborate upon this on the basis of the purport of Master Zhou's Explanation of the Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate (Taijitu shuo).

Where there is the Non-Ultimate and the Supreme Ultimate, there are yin and yang and the Five Phases; through the marvelous union of their true essences, human beings and myriad things are generated. Human beings receive the finest essence of the Five Phases and are indeed the most sentient of the myriad things. Yet among them, hardness and softness vary in ten thousand ways; feelings and desires stir one another, and advantage and harm contend with one another. Thus, although in the beginning each is endowed with the principle of the one Supreme Ultimate, when it comes to this point, there are those who cannot keep it whole. Only the sage receives the finest of the fine of the Five Phases: speaking of his psychophysical force (qi), it is supremely clear and bright; speaking of his physical constitution, it is supremely pure and unadulterated. 毫之偏倚焉而其發之也仁無一事之殘刻而其

而靜則亦何以為元而應事物之變哉靜者誠

…To harmonize the primal氣 in the golden tripod truly depends upon the meritorious aid of great Confucian scholars; to assist the transformative governance before the jade throne—how could the selection suitably fall upon the mediocre and ordinary? As heavenly favor repeatedly descends upon us, we tremble as if treading on thin ice.

This is indeed because we humbly encounter Your Majesty [〇〇〇〇], who are莊嚴, upright, balanced, and correct, civil, martial, sagely, and divine. You nurture the heavenly destiny to open it anew, and grasp the sovereign authority to make independent decisions. Appearing at the front platform of the hall to accept remonstrance, You bring about harmonious prosperity throughout the Four Seas; leaving Your seat vacant in eagerness to seek the worthy, You cherish the abundant flourishing of the millions of people. Whereas Your Majesty's sagely wisdom is able to combine the flourishing achievements of an entire era, we, your servants, weak and foolish, have suddenly disgraced the offices once held by those two worthies. In alarm, sweat drenches our backs; in shame, our faces grow ever thicker.

We, your servants, lack deep learning in the ways of Heaven and man, and our talents are like useless ailanthus and oak trees. In the past, when we shared duties in the Department and the Bureau, our repayment could not even amount to a drop of water or a grain of dust; now, promoted to hold the balance of state affairs, Your grace again surpasses mountains and peaks. 表稱

聞
策
第一問
袁芳

〔終以立人極貫之蓋得其要矣故表出之〕
考試官侍講呂批〔策答首問者槩騁浮詞陳腐可厭是篇簡而且精直而不倨良可嘉也〕

觀古今經世之典其名雖不同原古今經世之
典其道無二致蓋名不同者以刪述贊定制作
之有殊也道無二者以萬世天理民彝之不可
易也即萬世天理民彝之不可易以求刪述贊

觀古今經世之典，其名雖不同；原古今經世之典，其道無二致。蓋名不同者，以刪述、贊定、制作之有殊也；道無二者，以萬世天理、民彝之不可易也。即萬世天理、民彝之不可易，以求刪述、贊

… Imperial Majesty, overcome with the utmost emotion and trepidation, we reverently present this memorial of gratitude for Your Majesty's information.

Policy Essays
First Question
Yuan Fang 袁芳

title: 天順元年會試錄
text:
定制作之㫖則其所以立人極而化天下者一
而已矣又豈有異者哉粤稽諸古帝王之治天
下必有經世之典以立人極若伏羲之易四代
之書三百篇之詩魯之春秋先王之禮樂皆以
帝王所行之道載之典冊吾夫子因而刪定贊
述以立萬世之人極者也如易以道陰陽而乾
坤夫婦之道明書以道政事而君臣上下之分
定詩以備人倫春秋以明王道禮以秩天叙樂
以和民志是則六經名雖不同而明天理立人
===
極則一而已矣洪惟我
太祖高皇帝統一寰區稽古為治乃於萬機之暇
御製大誥三編頒布中外有申明五常之條五教
育民之訓曰五常曰五教即所謂萬古天理民
彝不可易之道與六經之道以立人極而化天
下者蓋越千世而同一轍也
太宗文皇帝御製為善陰隲孝順事實
宣宗章皇帝御製五倫書曰善曰孝曰五倫即天理
民彝之至近與

translation_en: … [expurgating, transmitting, praising,] establishing, and creating, then that by which they establish the ultimate standard for humanity and transform the world is one and the same; how could there be any difference? Examining antiquity, when emperors and kings governed the world, they necessarily possessed statecraft canons with which to establish the ultimate standard for humanity. Such were the Book of Changes (Yi) of Fuxi, the Book of Documents (Shu) of the Four Dynasties, the Book of Odes (Shi) in three hundred pieces, the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) of Lu, and the Record of Rites (Li) and Book of Music (Yue) of the former kings—all recorded in canonical documents the Way practiced by emperors and kings, and our Master [Confucius] accordingly expurgated, established, praised, and transmitted them in order to establish the ultimate standard for humanity for ten thousand generations. For instance, the Changes speaks of yin and yang, whereby the way of qian and kun and of husband and wife is made clear; the Documents speaks of affairs of government, whereby the distinction between ruler and minister, superior and inferior, is settled; the Odes provides completely for human relationships; the Spring and Autumn Annals clarifies the Kingly Way; the Rites orders the heavenly hierarchy; and the Music harmonizes the minds of the people. Thus, although the names of the Six Classics differ, in clarifying heavenly principle and establishing the ultimate standard for humanity, they are one and the same. Humbly reflecting on our Grand Progenitor, Emperor Gao [the Hongwu Emperor], when he unified the realm and examined antiquity to govern, in his leisure from the myriad affairs of state he imperially composed the three compilations of the Grand Pronouncements (Dagao) and promulgated them inside and outside the court, containing articles reiterating the Five Constant Virtues and instructions on the Five Teachings for educating the people. What are called the Five Constant Virtues and the Five Teachings are precisely what is meant by the unchanging Way of heavenly principle and the moral norms of the people for ten thousand ages; along with the Way of the Six Classics in establishing the ultimate standard for humanity and transforming the world, across a thousand generations they follow the exact same track. The Grand Ancestor, Emperor Wen [the Yongle Emperor], imperially composed the Hidden Rewards of Doing Good (Weishan yinzhi) and the True Records of Filial Piety and Obedience (Xiaoshun shishi), and the Proclaiming Ancestor, Emperor Zhang [the Xuande Emperor], imperially composed the Book of the Five Human Relationships (Wulun shu). … the articles on the Five Constant Virtues and the precepts of the Five Teachings in the Sacred Pronouncements, all follow the same path, and are in no way different from the Way of the Book of Changes (Yi), the Book of Documents (Shu), the Book of Odes (Shi), the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu), the Rites (Li), and Music (Yue). Second Policy Question

Comment by Associate Examiner and Acting Director Weng: Most writers in the examination hall are overly general and lack substance; when it comes to summarizing and covering the meaning in a single word, they are like chasing the wind and clutching at shadows, utterly lost with nowhere to turn. It ought to be singled out and published.

Comment by Examiner and Chancellor Xue: The books of the sages and worthies are rooted in a single principle. This policy essay is able to elucidate it; the author is truly a scholar of learning.

text:
論聖賢範世之書雖異原聖賢傳心之理則同
夫所以異者以範世之書也所以同者以傳心
之理也即其書之異而求其心之同則千古聖
賢之書無二致矣請因明問而陳之道陰陽者
易也道政事者書也理性情者非詩乎定名分
者非春秋乎定民志和民心者禮與樂也易之陽
為元亨陰為利貞元亨利貞即天命之賦於吾
心之仁義禮智也書之道心即吾心之天性也
詩之性情非吾心之性情乎春秋之名分皆君臣
===
父子之道又非吾心之秉彝乎禮之敬即吾心
之天理也樂之和即吾心之中和也大學之明
德論語之仁非吾心所具之理乎孟子之性善
中庸之中和又非吾心之性乎周子之太極即中
正仁義之性也通書之仁義禮智又所以明太
極之理也張子之西銘明理一而分殊理一非
仁乎分殊非義乎仁義又吾心之性也是則易
也書也詩也春秋也禮樂也四書也與夫周張
之書是其為教為書雖不同而其理一而已矣

中庸之中和又非吾心之性乎周子之太極即中
正仁義之性也通書之仁義禮智又所以明太
極之理也張子之西銘明理一而分殊理一非
仁乎分殊非義乎仁義又吾心之性也是則易
也書也詩也春秋也禮樂也四書也與夫周張
之書是其為教為書雖不同而其理一而已矣
punctuated: 論聖賢範世之書雖異，原聖賢傳心之理則同。夫所以異者，以範世之書也；所以同者，以傳心之理也。即其書之異，而求其心之同，則千古聖賢之書無二致矣。請因明問而陳之。道陰陽者，《易》也；道政事者，《書》也；理性情者，非《詩》乎？定名分者，非《春秋》乎？定民志、和民心者，《禮》與《樂》也。《易》之陽為元亨，陰為利貞，元亨利貞，即天命之賦於吾心之仁義禮智也。《書》之道心，即吾心之天性也。《詩》之性情，非吾心之性情乎？《春秋》之名分，皆君臣父子之道，又非吾心之秉彝乎？《禮》之敬，即吾心之天理也；《樂》之和，即吾心之中和也。《大學》之明德、《論語》之仁，非吾心所具之理乎？《孟子》之性善、《中庸》之中和，又非吾心之性乎？周子之《太極》，即中正仁義之性也；《通書》之仁義禮智，又所以明太極之理也。張子之《西銘》，明理一而分殊，理一非仁乎？分殊非義乎？仁義，又吾心之性也。是則《易》也、《書》也、《詩》也、《春秋》也、《禮》《樂》也、《四書》也，與夫周、張之書，是其為教、為書雖不同，而其理一而已矣。
translation_en:
When we discuss the books by which the sages and worthies modeled the world, they are different; yet when we trace the principle by which the sages and worthies transmitted the mind, it is the same. The reason they differ is that they are books for modeling the world; the reason they are the same is that they are the principle for transmitting the mind. If we approach the differences among their books and seek the sameness of their minds, then the books of the sages and worthies across a thousand ages have no two aims. Allow me to set this forth in response to the insightful question.

That which speaks of yin and yang is the Classic of Changes (Yi); that which speaks of affairs of governance is the Classic of Documents (Shu); is not that which regulates human nature and emotions the Classic of Odes (Shi)? Is not that which fixes names and obligations the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu)? That which settles the people's will and harmonizes the people's minds is the Classic of Rites (Li) and the Classic of Music (Yue). In the Changes, yang is origination and flourishing (yuan heng), and yin is advantage and correctness (li zhen); origination, flourishing, advantage, and correctness are none other than the benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom conferred upon our minds by the Mandate of Heaven. The "mind of the Way" (daoxin) in the Documents is none other than the heavenly nature of our mind. Are not the nature and emotions in the Odes the nature and emotions of our mind? The names and obligations in the Spring and Autumn Annals, which are all the Way of ruler and minister, father and son—are they not also the constant norms (bingyi) of our mind? Reverence in the Rites is none other than the heavenly principle of our mind; harmony in the Music is none other than the centrality and harmony (zhonghe) of our mind. Are not the "illustrious virtue" (mingde) of the Great Learning (Daxue) and the "benevolence" (ren) of the Analects (Lunyu) the principle endowed within our mind? Are not the "goodness of human nature" (xingshan) of the Mencius (Mengzi) and the "centrality and harmony" of the Doctrine of the Mean (Zhongyong) also the nature of our mind? Master Zhou's [Zhou Dunyi 周敦頤] Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate (Taiji) is none other than the nature of centrality, correctness, benevolence, and righteousness; the benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom of his Penetrating the Classic of Changes (Tongshu) are in turn that by which the principle of the Supreme Ultimate is elucidated. Master Zhang's [Zhang Zai 張載] Western Inscription (Ximing) elucidates that principle is one while its manifestations are distinct (li yi er fen shu). Is not the oneness of principle benevolence? Is not the distinction of manifestations righteousness? Benevolence and righteousness are also the nature of our mind. Thus, the Changes, the Documents, the Odes, the Spring and Autumn Annals, the Rites and Music, the Four Books, together with the writings of Masters Zhou and Zhang—although as teachings and as books they are not the same, their principle is simply one and nothing more.

title: 天順元年會試錄
text:
明問謂朱子言孟子之性善可以貫通七篇之
義然人性上不容一物而千古聖賢之書
性之一言皆足以涵蓋其義又豈特七篇而已
哉不然張子何以又曰性者萬物之一原謹以
是為終篇獻
第三問
黎淳
同考試官員外郎沈批此策善於發明超出眾
作博學之士也高薦何忝
===
同考試官典籍徐批為治之法本於為治之道實萬世
不易之良規此卷得之誠有學有識之士也宜置選列
同考試官脩撰岳批策能詳於制度必稽古之
士也擢置選列當適於用
考試官侍講呂批此策歷叙古今亹亹不竭而
又以徒善徒法發揚餘意有用世之學者歟
考試官學士薛批自古之為治只有道與法二
者雖不可相無但道為之本耳此策以常經
通誼貫篇意最是篇終引程子言明本重於法

第三問
黎淳

translation_en:
The sagacious question states that Master Zhu [Zhu Xi] said Mencius's doctrine of the goodness of human nature can thread together the meaning of all seven books of the Mencius. Yet nothing extraneous can be added onto human nature, and as for the books of the sages and worthies across all antiquity, the single word "nature" is sufficient to encompass the meaning of them all—how could it be limited to the seven books alone? Otherwise, why would Master Zhang [Zhang Zai] also say, "Human nature is the single source of the myriad things"? I respectfully offer this to conclude my essay.

title: 天順元年會試錄
text:
王道分明可見非老於學有不及此
嘗謂帝王之治天下有天地之常經有古今之
通誼天地之常經為治之道也道則萬古而不
易古今之通誼為治之法也法則因時以制宜
有治道以建天下之大本有治法以成天下之
大務斯可以言治矣粵稽諸古人心惟危道心
惟微惟精惟一允執其中者堯舜禹之治道也
懋昭大德建中于民皇建有極斂時五福者成
湯文武之治道也惟其一中授受而道無不全
===
是以創制立度而法無不備焉分五服則甸侯
綏要荒有其制矣爵五等則公侯伯子男有其
等矣建百官則唐虞官百庶政惟和夏商官倍
亦克用乂焉修五禮則祭祀有儀服制有等軍
旅有數宴享有節婚姻以時焉審律呂而章韶
夏濩武之樂以興定田賦而貢助徹之法以立
庠序學校之異名瞽宗辟雍之異制者設學校
以育賢也敷納以言明試以功鄉舉里選賓興
賢能者慎選舉以用人也一德一心而徂征有

… whereby the Kingly Way can be clearly seen; no one who is not deeply seasoned in learning could attain to this.

I have held that in the governance of all under Heaven by emperors and kings, there is the constant standard of Heaven and Earth, and there is the universal appropriateness of past and present. The constant standard of Heaven and Earth is the Way of governance, and the Way remains unchanging for ten thousand ages; the universal appropriateness of past and present is the method of governance, and methods are tailored to suit the times. Only when there is the Way of governance to establish the great foundation of the realm, and the methods of governance to accomplish the great affairs of the realm, can one speak of true governance. Examining antiquity: "The human mind is precarious, the mind of the Way is subtle; be discerning, be undivided, and sincerely hold fast the Mean"—this was the Way of governance of Yao, Shun, and Yu. "Strenuously make illustrious great virtue, and establish the Mean among the people," and "The sovereign establishes the supreme standard, and gathers in the Five Blessings"—this was the Way of governance of Tang the Completer, King Wen, and King Wu. Precisely because this single Mean was transmitted and received so that the Way lacked nothing in completeness, when institutions were created and regulations established, the methods likewise lacked nothing in thoroughness. In dividing the Five Dependencies, there were the regulations for the Royal Domain, the侯 (Lord's) Zone, the Pacified Zone, the Controlled Zone, and the Wild Zone; in conferring the five ranks of nobility, there were the grades of duke, marquis, earl, viscount, and baron; in establishing the hundred offices, "Tang and Yu had a hundred officials, and the numerous affairs of government were harmonious; Xia and Shang doubled the officials, and were likewise able to maintain order"; in cultivating the Five Rites, sacrifices had their ceremonies, mourning garments had their grades, military expeditions had their numbers, banquets and offerings had their measure, and marriages followed their proper seasons. By examining the pitch-pipes, the music of Da Zhang, Da Shao, Da Xia, Da Huo, and Da Wu arose; by fixing land taxes, the systems of tribute (gong), aid (zhu), and sharing (che) were established. The different names of xiang, xu, xue, and xiao, and the different institutions of the Guzong and Biyong, were the establishment of schools to nurture the worthy; "receiving reports in words and clearly testing by achievements," recommending candidates from districts and villages, and presenting the worthy and able as guests to the court, were the careful selection of officials so as to employ men. title: 天順元年會試錄
text:
苗六鄉六遂而寓兵於農其立兵制為何如刑
期無刑而欽哉惟恤式敬由獄而列用中罰其
明刑罰又何如唐虞三代為治之法至精至密
然亦莫非聖人執中建極以為之本是宜當時
庶績咸熙而四方有風動之休萬民咸若而比
屋有可封之俗也三代而下言治者必曰漢唐
宋夫大封同姓詔定元功地分十道各有節度
非不封建也果能如先王之封建乎漢制九卿
又立三公唐設六部又有九寺非無官制也果
===
能如先王之官制乎孫叔通之起朝儀祖孝孫
之進雅樂陳祥道之定禮書禮樂非不詳也限
田代田之有規租庸調法之有目口分世業之
有條田賦非不定也然則制度之末而已耳三
雍學舍之增築三館六學之增廣學校非不興
也三經十科之辟召六科四事之銓選選舉非
不嚴也亦特文為之具而已耳至若漢唐之八
校府兵宋之三衙四廂而兵有其制漢之約法
三章唐之律令格式而刑有其等嗟夫漢唐宋為
