translation_en:
… the Youmiao, and through the Six Districts (liuxiang) and Six Outlying Areas (liusui) embedding soldiers among the farmers—how was their establishment of military institutions? Aiming through punishments to reach an end to punishments, saying "Be reverent, be compassionate!", and using reverence in judicial cases while applying measured penalties—how too was their clarification of punishments and penalties? The methods of governance of Tang, Yu, and the Three Dynasties were utmost in precision and density, yet none failed to take the sages' holding fast to the Mean and establishing the Supreme Ultimate as their foundation. It was fitting that at the time all achievements were resplendent and the four quarters enjoyed the blessing of being moved as by the wind; the myriad people were all compliant and house by house possessed customs worthy of enfeoffment.

After the Three Dynasties, those who speak of governance inevitably name the Han, Tang, and Song. Now, grandly enfeoffing those of the same surname and issuing edicts to settle the ranking of founding merits, or dividing the land into ten circuits each with its Military Commissioner (jiedu)—it is not that they did not practice enfeoffment, but could it truly compare to the enfeoffment of the Former Kings? The Han instituted the Nine Ministers (jiuqing) and also established the Three Dukes (sangong); the Tang set up the Six Ministries (liubu) and also had the Nine Courts (jiusi)—it is not that they lacked an official system, but could it truly compare to the official system of the Former Kings? With Sun Shutong [Shusun Tong 叔孫通] instituting court ceremonial, Zu Xiaosun 祖孝孫 presenting elegant music, and Chen Xiangdao 陳祥道 compiling the treatise on rites (Lishu), rites and music were not lacking in detail; with the regulations for land limitation (xiantian) and alternating fields (daitian), the headings of the grain-labor-cloth tax system (zuyongdiao fa), and the articles on personal-share (koufen) and hereditary-estate (shiye) lands, land and taxation were not unsettled—yet these were merely the superficialities of institutions. With the additional construction of the Three Imperial Academies (sanyong) and school buildings, and the expansion of the Three Institutes (sanguan) and Six Schools (liuxue), schools were not unprosperous; with recruitment by summons in the Three Classics and Ten Categories, and selection and appointment by the Six Categories and Four Criteria, selection and recommendation were not lax—yet these too were merely formal instruments. As for the Eight Colonels (baxiao) and Garrison Militia (fubing) of the Han and Tang, and the Three Metropolitan Commands (sanya) and Four Quarters (sixiang) of the Song, the military had its system; with the Han pact of three articles of law, and the statutes (lü), ordinances (ling), regulations (ge), and ordinances of procedure (shi) of the Tang, punishments had their gradations. Alas! The methods of governance of the Han, Tang, and Song…

title: 天順元年會試錄
text:
言論皆至理所寓苟不即物即事以窮其理則
何以析之極其精而不亂合之盡其大而無餘
哉此格物致知誠吾儒第一事也且嘗觀夫物
之至大者天地也其未闢之前雖無圖書之可
紀而實有理數之可推邵子即理數以推之則
天開於子地闢於丑者可知矣理之至精者太
極也太極未動之前即太極靜而陰也陰之前
又太極動而陽也動靜無端隂陽無始則太極
未動之前為太極之靜者可知矣至於日者陽
===
之精月者陰之精月本無光受日以為光方三
日月生明之時日在其西以其光載於月魄漸
滿而至於望及既望之後日在其東則月光漸
虧其西而日光終守其東以至於晦是則月遡
日於西則西明遡日於東則東明日月相望則
其光滿其曰載者加載之載如韓文以孺子載
劉章從謁者載侯嬴直上載之載盖以其光加
於月魄也其曰終者終守月之魄於東也其曰
遡者迎日之光以為明也天地定位山澤通气

translation_en: …discussions are all where the ultimate principle resides. If one does not approach things and affairs to exhaustively investigate their principles, then how could one analyze them to the utmost subtlety without confusion, and synthesize them to the fullest magnitude without omission? Thus the investigation of things and extension of knowledge is truly the foremost task of us Confucians. Moreover, let us observe that which is the greatest of things: heaven and earth. Before their opening and formation, although there were no diagrams or writings to record them, there were indeed principles and numbers by which they could be deduced. Master Shao [Shao Yong 邵雍] deduced them from principles and numbers, and thus that heaven opened at the zi epoch and earth formed at the chou epoch can be known. That which is the most subtle of principles is the Supreme Ultimate (Taiji). Before the Supreme Ultimate moved, it was simply the Supreme Ultimate in stillness, which is yin; before yin, it was again the Supreme Ultimate in movement, which is yang. Movement and stillness have no beginning point, yin and yang have no start; thus that what preceded the movement of the Supreme Ultimate was the stillness of the Supreme Ultimate can be known. As for the sun, it is the essence of yang, and the moon is the essence of yin. The moon originally has no light, but receives the sun's light as its own. On the third day of the month, when the moon begins to grow bright, the sun is to its west, and loads its light onto the dark disk of the moon, which gradually fills until the full moon (wang). After the full moon, the sun is to its east, so the moon's light gradually wanes on its west, while the sun's light holds to the end on its east until the dark of the moon (hui). Thus when the moon faces the sun in the west, its western side is bright; when it faces the sun in the east, its eastern side is bright; and when the sun and moon stand opposite each other, its light is full. What is called "loading" (zai 載) means zai in the sense of placing or carrying a load upon—like the zai in Han Yu's 韓愈 prose "carrying the child," Liu Zhang's 劉章 "riding with the internuncio," or Hou Ying's 侯嬴 "mounting straight into the carriage"—meaning that the sun places its light upon the dark disk of the moon. What is called "holding to the end" (zhong 終) means holding to the dark disk of the moon in the east until the end. title: 天順元年會試錄
text:
雷風相薄水火不相射與夫天地定位否泰反
類山澤通氣損咸見義風雷相薄恒益起意水
火相射既濟未濟以及八卦成列之四圖乃伏
羲先天圖也是圖自孔子之後隱於異學邵康
節得之李之才出於陳希夷易中一字一義皆出於
此故邵子曰圖雖無文吾終日言未甞離乎是
至程子作易傳而無一語及之者蓋程邵雖同
時而程子未甞問及邵子而邵子亦弗之言所
以程子之作易傳只自乾之彖元亨利貞以下
===
故朱子曰邵傳羲畫程演周經者此也至於羲
之卦禹之疇皆因河圖洛書以畫以叙固不待
言矣而周子作太極圖則以心契造化之妙自
一理陰陽五行以及於男女萬物發天地萬物
之秘又豈待取法河圖洛書乎然周子雖未甞
取法於圖書而其曰太極者即圖書之虚其中
也其曰陰陽五行者即圖書之竒偶五行也而
其理又豈有異乎然朱子始言周子作太極圖
不繇師傳心與道妙至其晚年再定周子事狀

After Confucius, these diagrams were hidden away among heterodox teachings. Shao Kangjie (Shao Yong 邵雍) obtained them from Li Zhicai 李之才, deriving them ultimately from Chen Xiyi (Chen Tuan 陳摶). Every word and every meaning in the Book of Changes (Yi) comes from these. Therefore Master Shao said, "Although the diagrams have no words, though I speak all day long, I never depart from them." When it came to Master Cheng (Cheng Yi 程頤) composing the Commentary on the Changes (Yizhuan), he did not mention a single word about them. This is because although Cheng and Shao were contemporaries, Master Cheng never asked Master Shao about them, and Master Shao likewise did not speak of them; thus in composing the Commentary on the Changes, Master Cheng began only from "supreme,亨 [penetrating], advantageous, and correct" in the Judgment (Tuan) on the Qian hexagram and what follows. Therefore Master Zhu (Zhu Xi 朱熹) said, "Shao transmitted the trigrams of Fuxi, while Cheng expounded the classic of Zhou"—this is what he meant. As for the trigrams of Fuxi and the divisions of Yu, that they were drawn and arranged in accordance with the Yellow River Diagram (Hetu) and the Luo River Writing (Luoshu) goes without saying. Yet when Master Zhou (Zhou Dunyi 周敦頤) created the Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate (Taiji tu), his mind tallied with the marvels of creation; from the One Principle, yin and yang, and the Five Phases down to male and female and the myriad things, he revealed the secrets of heaven, earth, and the myriad things—so how could he have needed to model it upon the Yellow River Diagram and the Luo River Writing? Nevertheless, although Master Zhou never modeled his work on the Diagram and the Writing, what he called the Supreme Ultimate is none other than the empty center of the Diagram and the Writing; and what he called yin and yang and the Five Phases are none other than the odd and even numbers and the Five Phases of the Diagram and the Writing. How, then, could their principles be any different? title: 天順元年會試錄
text:
乃謂張忠定公言公事未着字為陽已着字為
陰之說恐其傳亦遠有端緒故與初說不能無
異也若夫本然之性有善無惡此固然也至張
子有曰形而後有氣質之性善反之則天地之
性存程子曰論性不論氣不備論氣不論性不
明然氣質之性即本然之性墮於氣質之中
者故有昏明強弱之不同非有二性也若太極
圖無極而太極即本然之性其太極在陰陽五
行之中有善有惡者氣質之性也此氣質之論
===
與圖相合者如此雖然天地日月陰陽也河圖
洛書陰陽也羲之畫易之書程之傳張忠定公
之言周子之圖程張氣質之論皆發明陰陽之
理也理者何太極是也所謂析之極其精而不
亂合之盡其大而無餘於此庶可見矣謹以是
為對
第五問
楊冕

乃謂張忠定公言「公事未着字為陽，已着字為陰」之說，恐其傳亦遠有端緒，故與初說不能無異也。若夫本然之性，有善無惡，此固然也。至張子有曰：「形而後有氣質之性，善反之則天地之性存。」程子曰：「論性不論氣，不備；論氣不論性，不明。」然氣質之性，即本然之性墮於氣質之中者，故有昏明強弱之不同，非有二性也。若《太極圖》無極而太極，即本然之性；其太極在陰陽五行之中，有善有惡者，氣質之性也。此氣質之論與圖相合者如此。雖然，天地日月，陰陽也；河圖洛書，陰陽也。羲之畫、《易》之書、程之《傳》、張忠定公之言、周子之《圖》、程張氣質之論，皆發明陰陽之理也。理者何？太極是也。所謂析之極其精而不亂，合之盡其大而無餘，於此庶可見矣。謹以是為對。

translation_en:
…he then cited the saying of Duke Zhongding of Zhang (Zhang Yong 張詠) that "official business before a signature has been affixed is yang, and after a signature has been affixed is yin," suspecting that the transmission of this teaching also had distant origins, and thus it could not help differing somewhat from his earlier view. As for original nature (benran zhi xing), that it possesses goodness and no evil is certainly true. Yet Master Zhang (Zhang Zai 張載) said: "Only after physical form exists is there physical nature (qizhi zhi xing); if one skillfully returns to the source, then the nature of Heaven and Earth is preserved." Master Cheng said: "To discuss nature without discussing vital force (qi) is incomplete; to discuss vital force without discussing nature is unclear." However, physical nature is simply original nature after it has fallen into the midst of physical constitution, which is why there are differences of obscurity and clarity, strength and weakness—not that there are two separate natures. In terms of the Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate (Taijitu), the Non-Ultimate and yet Supreme Ultimate is original nature; that the Supreme Ultimate resides amid yin and yang and the Five Phases, where there is both good and evil, is physical nature. Such is the way this discourse on physical constitution accords with the Diagram. Even so, Heaven and Earth, the sun and the moon, are yin and yang; the River Chart (Hetu) and the Luo Writing (Luoshu) are yin and yang. The trigrams drawn by Fuxi, the Book of Changes (Yi), the Commentary (Zhuan) of Master Cheng, the words of Duke Zhongding of Zhang, the Diagram of Master Zhou, and the discourses of Masters Cheng and Zhang on physical constitution all elucidate the principle of yin and yang. And what is this principle? It is the Supreme Ultimate. What is meant by "analyzing it to the utmost subtlety without confusion, and synthesizing it to the fullest magnitude without omission" may perhaps be seen right here. I respectfully offer this as my reply.

… be ranked among the coadjutors of the Three Kings. Since Your Excellency has condescended to inquire about the talent required of a king's coadjutor, this student begs leave to set the matter forth point by point.

Where there is the learning of sages and worthies, there will be the achievements of sages and worthies—this is a necessary principle. Thus, in the single book Both Possessed Pure Virtue (Xian you yi de), how great was the learning of Yi Yin 伊尹! Consequently, he was able to accomplish the meritorious work of making his ruler and people like Yao 堯 and Shun 舜. In the three chapters of the Charge to Yue (Yue ming), how great was the learning of Fu Yue 傅說! Consequently, he was able to achieve the service of being the "seasonable rain" and the "salt and plum." Assisting Kings Wen 文 and Wu 武 to settle the great enterprise, and aiding Kings Cheng 成 and Kang 康 to bring about Great Peace—how flourishing were the achievements of the Duke of Zhou 周公! If we examine such texts as the Officers of Zhou (Zhou guan) and the Establishment of Government (Li zheng), his learning can be known. How magnificent were the accomplishments of the Duke of Shao 召公! If we examine such chapters as the Announcement of the Duke of Shao (Shao gao) and the Hounds of Lü (Lü ao), his learning can be seen. These four dukes were all the outstanding figures of their ages, which is why they are called the coadjutors of the Three Kings without any cause for shame.

As for Master Yan (Yanzi 顏子, Yan Hui 顏回), he followed and studied with the Sage, living in a mean alley with a single bamboo dish of rice and a gourd dipper of drink, and nothing more. As for Kongming 孔明 (Zhuge Liang 諸葛亮), he went forth to serve the Former Lord (Liu Bei 劉備) and was the worthy coadjutor of a single state, and nothing more. Yet commentators have all accorded them the talent of a king's coadjutor. When a gentleman compares men, he must match them only with their proper peers. If one calls Kongming a king's coadjutor, Kongming's enterprise remained unfulfilled; if one calls Master Yan a king's coadjutor, Master Yan's obscurity and poverty were extreme. To object on such grounds is doubtless to judge by their outward achievements without tracing their learning, and to look at their station without seeking their minds.

二表》之學，與《伊訓》、《說命》同一淵源也；而鞠躬盡瘁之心，實符於赤舄之几几。謂孔明為王佐，愚於程子之論愈無疑矣。向使天若興周，顏子將有以復西周之盛；天若祚漢，孔明將有以興三代之治矣。然二子雖俱見許於先儒，而顏子亞聖，恐非可與孔明例論也。

執事又謂：士大夫學先正之道，當讀何書、明何理、為何事，而可以幾於先正？愚以為，書者載道之具，道者致澤之本。書莫大於《五經》、《四書》，其所載者，皆脩、齊、治、平之道也。亦曰從事於此，以明其理，為其事，竭忠盡力，以脩人臣之道，庶幾古人於萬一耳。謹對。

… the learning embodied in the Two Memorials on Sending Out the Troops (Chushi erbiao) shares the very same fountainhead as the Instructions of Yi (Yixun) and the Charge to Yue (Yueming); and his heart of bending his body and exhausting his strength until death truly accords with the serene composure of the red slippers [of the Duke of Zhou]. As for calling Kongming [Zhuge Liang 諸葛亮] an assistant to a true king, I have all the less doubt about Master Cheng's assessment. Had Heaven wished to revive the Zhou, Master Yan [Yan Hui 顏回] would have had the wherewithal to restore the flourishing of the Western Zhou; had Heaven blessed the Han, Kongming would have had the wherewithal to revive the governance of the Three Dynasties. Yet although both men were commended by former Confucians, Master Yan was a Second Sage (yasheng) and, I fear, cannot be discussed on the same level as Kongming.

You, sir, further ask: if scholar-officials wish to study the Way of the former worthies, what books should they read, what principles should they clarify, and what affairs should they undertake so that they might approach the former worthies? In my humble view, books are the instruments that convey the Way, and the Way is the foundation for bringing blessings to the people. Among books, none are greater than the Five Classics and the Four Books, and what they record are all the Ways of cultivating the self, regulating the family, governing the state, and bringing peace to the world. One need only devote oneself to these so as to clarify their principles and undertake their affairs, exhausting one's loyalty and strength to cultivate the Way of a minister, and thus perhaps come within one part in ten thousand of the ancients. I respectfully reply.

translation_en:
Postface to the Record of the Metropolitan Examination

At the outset of when the Sacred Son of Heaven, his virtue harmonizing with Heaven, grandly received the Mandate of Heaven's assistance and succeeded in restoring the Precious Throne, the Way of Heaven became clear, the Way of Earth became tranquil, and the Way of Man became rectified. Throughout the civilized central lands and among the barbarous tribes, there was none who did not rejoice and dance with excitement, like beholding the sun and moon after prolonged gloom, or receiving unceasing rain after a long drought. How much more so for those scholars who had been storing up their talents while awaiting the right time! Raising their heads toward the radiance of the Imperial virtue, and regarding this as an opportunity that comes once in a thousand years, who among them would not wish to set forth what they have learned so as not to fail this enlightened era?

In the second month of spring of the first year of the Tianshun reign [1457], because the Tribute Scholars from across the realm who had come for the Metropolitan Examination numbered over three thousand, the Ministry of Rites, in accordance with established statutes, memorialized to request the appointment of officials to serve as Examiners. title: 天順元年會試錄
text:
眾執事皆遴選以往且承
詔旨毋限以額必欲得真才為
用由是若內若外祗若
聖意咸秉至公以是月癸卯丙午
己酉分三場鎖院命題而試
之防範周密品式具備臣等
夙興夜寐鑒别惟懼弗精乃
===
即諸士子所作經義論策求
其能究聖賢之指達時措之
宜者得若干人既而列次其
名氏復取其文之理明而事
實者載之于錄僉謂臣當為
後序以紀
國家得賢之盛臣嘗觀之自古

translation_en: …all the various functionaries were carefully selected to go forth. Moreover, we received an imperial decree not to restrict the quota, as His Majesty was determined to obtain genuine talent for employment. Consequently, both those within and without the examination compound reverently conformed to the Sacred Intention, all upholding the utmost impartiality. On the guimao, bingwu, and jiyou days of this month, the candidates were divided into three sessions, the compound was locked, and questions were set to test them; the security precautions were thorough and the regulations and formats were complete. Your servants rose early and retired late, fearing only that our discernment might lack precision. Accordingly, we examined the expositions on the Classics, discourses, and policy essays composed by the candidates, seeking those able to fathom the intentions of the sages and worthies and to grasp what is appropriate to implement for the times, thereby obtaining a certain number of men. Thereafter, having ranked their names in order, we further selected those compositions whose principles were clear and whose facts were substantive, and recorded them in the examination register. Everyone said that your servant ought to write the postface in order to record the flourishing state of the dynasty's acquisition of worthies. Your servant has observed that since antiquity…

title: 天順元年會試錄
text:
以来君天下者其治道之隆
莫不本於賢才之衆故帝舜
之盛也以黎獻共臣文王之
盛也以多士濟濟今
聖天子中天下定四海之一初凡
畜悳包道之士或郡縣賓興
或胄監儲育者靡不拔茅連
茹兾掇巍科以應時需正易
所謂雲從龍風從虎聖人作
而萬物覩何其盛哉雖然諸
士子既已擢秀於鄉試得雋
於會試行見
聖天子又將臨軒親策有臚傳之
典有錫宴之榮有觀政授職
alt_text:
以來君天下者其治道之隆
莫不本於賢才之衆故帝舜
之盛也以黎獻共臣文王之
盛也以多士濟濟今
聖天子中天下定四海之一初凡
蓄惠包道之士或郡縣賓興
或冑監儲育者靡不技茅連
===
茹彙援魏科以應時需正易
所謂雲從龍風從虎聖人作
而萬物覩何其盛哉雖然諸
士子既已擢秀於鄉試得儁
於會試行見
聖天子又將臨軒親策有臚傳之
典有錫宴之榮有觀政授職
punctuated: 以来，君天下者，其治道之隆，莫不本於賢才之衆。故帝舜之盛也，以黎獻共臣；文王之盛也，以多士濟濟。今聖天子中天下、定四海之一初，凡畜悳包道之士，或郡縣賓興，或胄監儲育者，靡不拔茅連茹，兾掇巍科，以應時需。正《易》所謂「雲從龍，風從虎，聖人作而萬物覩」，何其盛哉！雖然，諸士子既已擢秀於鄉試，得雋於會試，行見聖天子又將臨軒親策，有臚傳之典，有錫宴之榮，有觀政授職
translation_en: … times on down, for those who have ruled as sovereign over All under Heaven, the flourishing of their Way of governance has without exception been rooted in a multitude of worthy talents. Thus the flourishing of Emperor Shun was due to the eminent worthies among the multitude serving together as his ministers, and the flourishing of King Wen was due to the stately abundance of his many scholars. Now, at the very beginning of the Sacred Son of Heaven's standing at the center of All under Heaven and bringing stability to all within the Four Seas, all scholars who cherish virtue and embrace the Way—whether presented as honored guests from the prefectures and counties or nurtured and educated in the Directorate of Education—have without exception come forward together like couch-grass pulled up by the roots, hoping to pluck high examination honors in order to meet the needs of the times. This is precisely what the Book of Changes (Yi) calls "Clouds follow the dragon, winds follow the tiger; the Sage arises and all things behold him"—how flourishing indeed! Even so, now that the scholars have already been selected as the finest in the Provincial Examination and have won distinction in the Metropolitan Examination, before long the Sacred Son of Heaven will again appear in person at the palace to put his policy questions to them; there will be the ceremony of the roll-call announcement of the successful candidates, the glory of the bestowal of banquets, and the gradual progression of observing administration and being appointed to office…

title: 天順元年會試錄
text:
之漸尚當益加砥礪丕圖報
稱而不負其所學于以致吾
君於舜文措斯世於雍熙泰和之
盛若然則天下皆仰之曰此
天順初科所取真才碩賢也
豈惟今日仰之將千萬世仰
之而無窮矣書曰惟后非賢
===
不乂惟賢非后不食諸士子
今遭遇之盛如此可不以書
之所言而自期待也歟
奉議大夫通政使司左參議
兼翰林院侍講呂原謹序

奉議大夫通政使司左參議
兼翰林院侍講呂原謹序
punctuated:
之漸。尚當益加砥礪，丕圖報稱，而不負其所學，于以致吾君於舜、文，措斯世於雍熙泰和之盛。若然，則天下皆仰之曰：「此天順初科所取真才碩賢也！」豈惟今日仰之，將千萬世仰之而無窮矣。《書》曰：「惟后非賢不乂，惟賢非后不食。」諸士子今遭遇之盛如此，可不以《書》之所言而自期待也歟？
奉議大夫、通政使司左參議兼翰林院侍講呂原謹序。
translation_en:
…progression [of traineeship and appointment to office]. Still, they ought all the more to temper and refine themselves, grandly planning to requite the favor they have received and match the expectations placed upon them, so as not to betray what they have learned—thereby elevating our Sovereign to the level of Shun and King Wen, and placing this age in the flourishing state of harmonious peace and supreme concord. If so, then all under Heaven will look up to them and say: "These are the true talents and great worthies selected in the first examination of the Tianshun era!" Not only will people look up to them today, they will look up to them for ten thousand generations without end. The Book of Documents (Shu) says: "The sovereign without the worthy cannot govern; the worthy without the sovereign cannot be sustained." Having met with such splendid fortune today, how could you scholars not hold yourselves to the expectations set forth in the Book of Documents?

Respectfully written as a postface by Lü Yuan 呂原, Grand Master for Proper Consultation, Left Vice Commissioner in the Office of Transmission, concurrently Expositor-in-waiting in the Hanlin Academy.
